i am speaking today to bring to your attention the situation of romanian farmers today, one year after our accession to the european union. agriculture is still inefficient or too inefficient in romania and yet vital for a large part of the population. we have a large share of farmers in the total employed population, but also a large number of elderly farmers. in this context, i welcome the commission's decision not to activate the safeguard clause in this area; but that's not enough. payments from european funds will be only 25% of the european average in 2008. it takes nine years to touch it. in recent years, romania has been rapidly transposing the community acquis in the field of quality, sanitation and phytosanitary matters. adaptation costs can be a significant obstacle to the achievement of common agricultural policy benefits by romanian farmers. romania is the second largest agricultural producer in central and eastern europe after poland and only the use of european funds can recover and use this potential intelligently.

on behalf of the pse group. the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation no 11/1960 on the elimination of discrimination in respect of transport rates and conditions requires operators of road, rail and inland waterway transport of goods within the community to provide information on the rates, applicable agreements, conditions of transport and the necessary accompanying documents. it is thus forbidden for operators to create discrimination by applying differentiated tariffs (and here i refer to the transport of the same product, in the same type of transport system, on the same route), but discrimination created by the country of destination or origin. this regulation is extremely important, but as it was initiated in 1960, an update was needed. the proposed amendment simplifies existing legislation and provides greater stability in terms of freight transport conditions. according to the statistics provided by the commission, it is true - as the commissioner said - that the activity of 300 000 transport operators will be affected, in practice, or so the regulation refers, and this amendment will reduce administrative expenditure at community level by approximately eur 160 million per year. the european parliament has set itself the goal of reducing the administrative burden on businesses by 25% by 2012. the proposal to amend the two regulations, as submitted by the commission, is part of the measures designed to achieve this objective. it is true, however, that the transport committee was referred to the codecision procedure, and article 75 (3) of the treaty does not allow this. that is why the proposal put forward by mr costa, the rapporteur, was adopted unanimously.

in writing. − the initiative to clarify the rules on airport charges and to develop non-discriminatory and transparent procedures for the calculation of these charges is welcome as it prevents abuses by airports with a dominant market position. this ensures transparency and continuous exchange of information between providers and beneficiaries of air transport services, both for individual airports and for airport networks. in addition, member states have the possibility to apply the provisions of this directive to other airports in their national territory, thus encouraging competition and, by implication, lower airport charges, to the benefit of end-users. by having common standards, passengers will benefit from similar services at the same prices and airports will manage all facilities and services strictly on a cost-effective basis. the creation of an independent national regulatory authority in each member state will ensure that these procedures are properly implemented. i am convinced that by adopting this regulation, those who will benefit most will be european citizens. it will also encourage the extension of investment to the aviation sector and increase safety, security and passenger confidence, which will make a significant contribution to the development of the european union's air transport sector in the long term.
in writing. the proposal for a regulation on the export and import of dangerous substances improves the way chemicals are used so that public health and the environment are more effectively protected. this is with a view to encouraging the shared responsibility of exporters and importers and supporting their cooperative efforts to ensure control over the international movement of dangerous chemicals. the new regulation amends the definition of exporter to include persons exporting these chemicals from the european union but not established in the union, thus ensuring effective control and surveillance of the flow of dangerous chemicals. the prior consent procedure, known as pic, for which certain chemicals require explicit authorisation from the importing country, also helps countries involved in trade to be better informed about dangerous chemicals that have been banned for environmental and public health reasons and that may enter the national territory of importing countries. however, the pic procedure is not a substitute for effective and robust national border controls and member states should cooperate to ensure the effective management of the movement of these dangerous products within their national territory.
we welcome the commission's good intentions, but its effectiveness may be questionable. to maximise the impact of policies and protect workers, accurate statistics on occupational diseases are needed. the data available is incomplete, underestimates the phenomena or ignores reality. women are the main victims of this deficiency. first, because they work more in the informal economy or the "grey economy". the effects of working conditions on health are not recorded at all in this sector. the existing legal framework preserves an approach that focuses on accidents and risks in the so-called 'heavy', male, branches of the economy. we call on the commission to take a closer look at the specific differences between men and women employees, to assess the availability of gender-segregated data and to look at the long-term effects and psychological consequences of work. to prove the relevance of the request, we invite you to a factory in the textile industry. hearing and vision can be severely affected, and circulatory diseases are very common. the statistics are ignoring the situation. it's a so-called "light" industry, where women work mostly, and the wages are low, and because there's no risk. thus, current statistics preserve historical inequalities between men and women, including the gender pay gap.

in writing. the regulation we are amending (1408/71) plays a very important role in the realisation of one of the four fundamental freedoms of the european union, namely freedom of movement. the free movement of labour throughout the european union must not be restricted either directly by restricting the categories of occupation to which nationals of other member states have access or indirectly by eroding the social rights enjoyed by foreign workers. the commission proposal, which is accompanied by parliament's amendments, will therefore determine precisely when citizens continue to enjoy the special benefits granted by the state of nationality, when these benefits can be exported, or whether other social schemes are applied which do not disadvantage the foreign national. in addition, by broadening the categories of employment contracts used in europe, a common understanding of what constitutes self-employment or authorised natural person status is needed. last but not least, i believe that this report contributes to guaranteeing the social rights of citizens working in another eu member state. the removal of the bottlenecks in the recognition of social rights will lead to more mobility in the european union and a higher level of employment.

mr president, roma are neither the successors of the ancient roman empire, nor the contemporary inhabitants of rome. they are neither a nation without a state nor a national minority. they are an ethnocultural community, still cherishing its tribal tradition, and a pan-european community which was kept in slavery in pre-modern and early modern europe, which was sent to extermination camps by the fascist regimes and enclosed in the states turned into prisons by the communist dictatorship. they became free european citizens after the end of the cold war and the first post-bipolar european union enlargement. being marginalised and excluded over the centuries, the roma community found itself excluded from european wealth and tried to protect itself by challenging the european order. today, now that europe is reconciled with itself, should it be reconciled with the roma population as well, or should it declare and treat the roma as second-class citizens who are again to be concentrated in some member states transformed into roma ghettos? to these questions there is a single answer: the roma issue is a european issue. it is not a simple issue but a huge challenge – a common challenge which we must cope with jointly. otherwise we will be unable to integrate the roma community into european society and bring it into the european order. this is a cultural and social matter. the european union should mobilise funds, develop programmes and organise specific institutional structures in order to assist the national authorities of the countries where the roma choose to settle in order to offer this community a decent material life, a proper education, a fair opportunity to compete with others, free of any discrimination, and a cohesive sense of their existence within european civilisation. we expect the european commission to take the right steps in that direction and to keep the european parliament fully informed on the progress achieved.
the reporter. - a year ago, in january 2007, in the same room, we celebrated the accession of romania and bulgaria to the european union. i was thinking about the new opportunities created both for the two new member states and for the european union as a whole. the need for active and consistent union involvement in the black sea area and the development of a genuine regional cooperation policy, comparable to those existing for the mediterranean and the northern dimension, was necessary and obvious. now, in january 2008, as rapporteur for black sea cooperation, i have the opportunity to open this debate in plenary to discuss the concrete recommendations of the european parliament for the development of black sea synergy proposed in april by the european commission. these recommendations are the result of a broad process of reflection and consultation with all interested colleagues, as well as independent experts and officials. the report underlines the strategic importance of the black sea region for the european union, while at the same time clearly defining the objective of cooperation policy in this area: the creation of a common area of security, democracy and prosperity. the report highlights the importance of regional cooperation in mobilising the 10 riparian countries for dialogue and joint action, which are characterised by their diversity but also by an enormous potential that we cannot ignore. a priority responsibility of the european union is therefore to take on the role of active promoter of regional cooperation in the black sea. the key question this report seeks to answer is: how can european regional cooperation policy in the black sea be strengthened and effectively implemented to achieve the objective of creating a common area of security, democracy and prosperity? first, we need the european union's actions to be consistent, firm and focused on concrete results. the report identifies three key aspects: the mobilisation of all relevant financial instruments, increased cooperation with other institutions and bodies in the region, and, last but not least, the monitoring of actions to ensure their continuity and effectiveness and the establishment of an action plan. the report also recommends that the european union focus on five priority areas. it is clear that the black sea region is of strategic importance for the european union's energy security and diversification and requires a comprehensive approach in this direction. but it is imperative that the european union goes beyond economic cooperation and aims as its overriding objective to create a region where stability, democracy and good governance prevail. the european union's policy in the black sea region will not be complete until the european union is deeply involved in resolving existing conflicts, and the development of civil society, human contacts and good neighbourly relations are essential in this direction. as we are also discussing mrs polfer's report on the south caucasus, and the countries of this region are part of the wider black sea area, i would like to welcome the preparation of this report. it is important that the main ideas of the two reports coincide and underline the importance of cooperation and dialogue between all states as a prerequisite for development and prosperity, but also the need for a consistent involvement of the european union. in conclusion, i would like to thank all those who contributed to the report on black sea synergy. i appreciated the spirit of cooperation and the unanimous support of my colleagues in all groups. i hope that this spirit will guide the european union and the states of the black sea region in their joint effort to develop regional cooperation in this area.
reporting for the opinion of the committee on industry, research and energy. − with the accession of romania and bulgaria, the union has become an important player in the black sea region. the region is of geostrategic importance for the energy security and diversification of the union's energy supply routes, due to its proximity to the caspian sea, the middle east and central asia. promoting the union's principles cannot be done at the level of political values alone. open and transparent markets in the region need to be encouraged. the itre committee underlines the importance of the nabucco project for the diversification of the union's energy sources and calls on the member states, together with its partners, to ensure its implementation. we welcome the appointment of a coordinator for this priority project of european interest. the development of the infrastructure of the community ports on the black sea and the danube is essential for international trade and for the transport of hydrocarbons in the region. the itre committee regrets the lack of coordination of investment in energy, transport and tourism projects in the region and draws attention to the danger of pollution in the black sea. recognising the importance of the black sea forum and the black sea economic cooperation organisation, the itre commission recommends the creation of an eu black sea dimension similar to the nordic dimension.

madam president, after more than a century and a half of neglect, the black sea area is again at the pinnacle of international economics and politics. this area is currently striving to reach a new balance following the entrance of new actors, the eu included, after being considered a closed lake for so many years during the cold war. after the commission’s communication entitled ‘black sea synergy: a new regional cooperation initiative’, the current first report in parliament is another step in the right direction. but unfortunately, both are still not enough. the lack of identity of the area itself and the traditional sensitivities of certain eu countries towards russia, both political (for example ukraine, moldova, the southern caucasus and the frozen conflicts) and economic (the increased european dependence on russian gas and the delicate status of the eu-turkey negotiations), are probably among the reasons why the eu has limited itself to synergy instead of strategy. while strategy means clear objectives, concrete means to attain them and, eventually, a detailed calendar, all tailored to the merit of the area itself, synergy suggests simply connecting to neighbouring areas of interest to the eu. a strategy could be arrived at through concrete measures on how the eu deals with a multitude of local organisations; on physically linking the area to the rest of the continent in which the river danube is crucial; and on strengthening the instrument of neighbourhood policy towards the black sea area, as suggested through my group’s amendments. in conclusion, one word on moldova, the last piece of continental latinity outside eu borders. although part of the same regrettable experience at the beginning of the second world war, moldova could not share the positive destiny of the three baltic countries after the cold war. i believe europe has a duty to correct that situation and thus continue to encourage and respond to moldova’s efforts to join the union. my hope is that her case will be finally judged on its own merit and not remain a de facto prisoner of other eu relations, no matter how strategic that relation might be.

the essence of the european neighbourhood policy is cooperation based on a set of common values and interests of the union with the countries to which it applies. it is necessary to strengthen an area of stable neighbours, which would favourably affect the internal security of the union and would be a precondition for the prosperity and economic development of those states. the south caucasus countries have some features that are indispensable for the success of european projects in key areas such as energy and transport. the geopolitical significance of these countries is linked to their strategic positioning in relation to the energy resources of central asia. the region is essential as a transit area and represents one of the few corridors that can allow the union to diversify its access to energy resources from the caspian region. possible alternative gas transit routes from the caspian sea and pipeline projects crossing the black sea depend to a large extent on stability in the south caucasus. the european union is not the only actor strategically looking at this area. in parallel, two other important international pioneers have developed consolidated initiatives in the region as well as long-term strategies. the united states has an energy security action plan that proposes to initiate and develop alternative routes for the transport of gas and oil. russia is already proposing and financing its own projects, consolidating its position in the central asian market. in the current context, where the importance of the energy issue and dependence on russia have become evident, the low level of european union involvement in the area may lead to negative consequences for all member states in the future. the european union must develop without delay a common energy security policy in which the member states renounce their individual interests and in which it is absolutely vital that the countries of the south caucasus be part of it.

in writing. while appreciating the concerns of the environment committee, we are concerned about the limited relevance of the indicators used in the algorithm for calculating the allocation of pollutant emission allowances. it is necessary to set correction coefficients to reflect differences in investment potential between member states with similar gdp but different socioeconomic outlooks. the level of investment needs certainly varies exponentially according to the stage of development at which a given region of europe is situated. the national budgetary effort required to keep emissions within the allocated limits will thus be burdened by the investment budget for re-technologization, and in economically deprived areas it will become an obstacle to alignment with european environmental standards. the principle of european solidarity can only be respected in its spirit if countries and regions whose development is below the european average are treated with due regard for their specific stage. in the name of the same principle, i hope that those of my german colleagues who have criticised the decision to relocate the nokia factory will find out and openly tell the workers who lost their jobs in bochum that the wages of romanian workers are ten times lower than theirs and that a liter of milk or a liter of petrol costs as much as in germany.

madam president, commissioner, postal services are extremely important for the economic and social life of human communities. we must therefore guarantee the accessibility of postal services, but above all we must ensure the quality of these services. the full liberalisation of the postal services market, including for items weighing less than 50 grams, will allow for increased competition, the emergence of new operators and the creation of jobs. but i want to stress a few important points. first, it is essential that universal service be guaranteed and that every citizen be able to receive his mail, whether he lives in a mountain-top hamlet or on an island. secondly, we must ensure decent working conditions for workers in this sector and, above all, there are social guarantees for jobs and incomes. thirdly, in order for member states to guarantee universal service, it is essential that they define as soon as possible the way in which universal service is financed. the directive gives flexibility to the member states. fourth, as we are increasingly living in a digital world, it is essential that postal operators diversify their activities to offer electronic services. some member states may have an additional two years until full liberalisation of postal services. however, regardless of when liberalisation takes place, it is essential that postal operators have an efficient management system to guarantee a high quality of these services.

in writing. the full liberalisation of postal services in the member states of the european union will have a positive impact not only on users and consumers of postal services, who will benefit from new, innovative services and reduced postal rates, but also on the economies of the member states as a whole. the draft directive under discussion is only complete in its current form, which allows for the extension of the deadline for the full opening of the postal services market in some member states. romania is among the beneficiaries of the new provisions decided by the european parliament. the romanian universal service provider is currently undergoing a restructuring process, according to a programme decided by the romanian government for the period 2007-2010, after which preparations for the liberalisation of the postal services market will take place. this succession in time will benefit the romanian consumer, leading to better quality services and an affordable price for them in view of the liberalisation of the market after 1 january 2013.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr guardans cambó, and the committee on international trade very much indeed for this very constructive report. it confirms that we share a common vision, both on the importance of a proactive market access strategy for european businesses and workers, and on the basic principles that should underlie this strategy. the priorities that are set out here – smes, barriers to services and investment, public procurement and ipr – are very much my priorities. that is the same message that the european council sent last june, and again in response to our progress report last month. we have built a strong new consensus on the importance of this work. at the heart of the global europe strategy that we launched in 2006 was the commitment both to keeping our own markets in europe open, and also to refocusing our resources on creating new opportunities for european workers and companies in the markets of our main trading partners. we can do that above all through a successful wto trade deal, but we can also do it through a new generation of free-trade agreements. it also means taking a more hard-headed approach to modern trade barriers, and especially non-tariff barriers which operate not at the border, but behind the border. europe’s workers and companies can compete almost anywhere if they are given a fair opportunity and a level playing field on which to compete. our job is to support them and provide them with a platform to do that, which means focusing on the barriers, conditions and discriminatory regulatory practices that operate against them and deny them that fair opportunity to compete and to trade. the challenge in 2007 has been to put this policy into practice. in particular, we have focused on strengthening our resources on the ground in our most important markets by creating market access teams that bring together a business, a member state and commission staff and experts. these are the people who really know the markets and who have a feel for the local politics and a clear sense of both what is necessary and what is possible. this has produced good results. in the last six months we have scored important successes in south america, central asia, south asia, japan and russia. we have also stepped up our cooperation with the united states on market access issues, which has been instrumental in some of these successes. we have also introduced an on-line complaint register for eu companies and launched real-time and monthly reporting on market access work. i therefore mildly disagree with the suggestion in the report that the commission has not done enough to bring out the full potential of this partnership during the launch phase. that does not mean either that i consider the collaboration to be perfect or that i feel in the least bit complacent about what we could do differently, and even better, than we are at the moment. i agree that this new strategy is a dynamic process which requires constant vigilance and constant commitment. frankly, it also needs some more high-profile advocates of what we are doing and how we are setting about pursuing our objectives, both in this house and also among the member states – people who believe in economic openness, but who are also not afraid to speak up for reciprocal market opening, especially amongst those emerging economies whose own growth is being driven by their access to our markets. that is right, that is fair and that is the principle of international trade that we believe in – that whilst we remain open to others they too should progressively open their markets to us if the principle of international trade is going to be well and properly served. i agree with the rapporteur when he calls on all stakeholders to participate actively in this partnership. we are continuing to improve our coordination work on the ground with member states and industry, but we need these experts to step up as well if we are to achieve our potential. on the question of resources, i am grateful for the additional staff that the budgetary authorities have allocated to dg trade. we will continue to push for more resources for the most important markets in asia and, for example, in brazil. in the mean time we have strengthened our staffing on market access activities in brussels. finally, i also take note of your request to receive an annual report from the commission. along with the regular reporting, i would be pleased to discuss the annual activity report with parliament. so, my thanks again to the rapporteur and to parliament for its engagement in this very important work. it is vital that we maintain our energy and engagement in 2008 and beyond. this priority means a lot to me and to my services; it means a lot to our businesses in europe and for the employment they are able to create for our workers, flowing from increased market access and from the strengthening of world trade that is at the heart of our trade policy strategy for a global europe. reporting for the opinion of the committee on industry, research and energy. - mr president, commissioner, the european union's strategy for market access was launched in 1996. the commission has developed a free service that provides european exporters with an up-to-date, public electronic register of market access conditions in some 100 countries. in 2007, the euro area trade surplus was eur 28.3 billion, compared with a deficit of eur 9.3 billion in 2006. the eu-27 recorded a deficit of eur 185.7 billion in 2007, compared with a deficit of eur 192.1 billion in 2006. so, at community level, measures must be taken to make the member states outside the euro area more competitive. we believe that market access will be facilitated by promoting the values and principles of the european union to third countries by promoting open markets, by bringing social and environmental standards closer together and by ensuring the protection of intellectual property rights. investments in research, promotional campaigns to make available services and information to the public, improvement of the community information system on market access, interconnection of specific databases and training of specialists to support european enterprises must form part of the commission's partnership with the member states and with european enterprises.
let me make a few remarks on the ce marking. at present, it applies to any product that is covered by a european directive. as long as manufacturers can mark most products without any verification by a third authority or an independent body, this marking will not prove effective. that's the first problem. we therefore all agree that the current system of ce marking of products is not able to guarantee safety for european consumers. in fact, it was not even designed with the intention of being a safety mark. commissioner verheugen, you said last year that we would never have 100% product safety. that is why i am calling on the european commission to consider, in addition to closer market surveillance and stricter customs controls, tougher sanctions for companies that produce or import products that do not comply with eu rules and directives. let us not forget that the vast majority of european consumers think uninformedly when they consider that a product bearing the ce marking is made in europe or has been certified by an independent european body. that's the second problem. even commissioner verheugen feels that the current ce marking may be a little confusing. this is unacceptable and i therefore ask the european commission to launch information campaigns for european consumers so that they do not confuse the ce marking with a quality and safety mark. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we all agree that there must be a safety mark. whether the current ce marking is improved or whether there is an additional marking, the solution must be found as soon as possible. the internal market implies not only the free movement of products but also the adoption of effective measures to protect consumers.

mr president, one of the key recommendations of the european parliament is to combat protectionism both within and outside the eu. i firmly believe that protectionism undermines, rather than defends, citizens’ rights, but that europe should be looking at its own backyard first. our highest priority should now be the removal of protectionist barriers within the eu. in order to make the european single market a reality we need to enhance the four fundamental freedoms of the common market, especially the free movement of workers. our report acknowledges that many labour markets remain segmented and that worker mobility is still low. how surprising! have we forgotten that most citizens of the new member states still need a permit to work in other eu countries? ladies and gentlemen, europe is currently facing considerable demographic challenges which will have a long-term impact on its future. today's debate is therefore not only welcome but also necessary to ensure a successful future and sustained development. among all the recommendations in the report, i believe that three ideas should form the core of european demographic policy. in the context of the ageing population, the european union must give particular attention to children and young people in the first place. the protection of the child and the provision of a solid opportunity for personal and professional development for young people are strategically important for the future, and the development of these objectives must be integrated into a comprehensive policy for the protection of the family and the promotion of women. the second element, education, is closely related to the principle mentioned above. a successful europe requires human resources capable of meeting new challenges, but also scientific progress, public health and a decent standard of living. achieving these objectives is indisputably dependent on the level of education and continuing training of all generations. finally, migration flows are the third decisive factor, with immigration being an important prerequisite for ensuring demographic balance and economic growth. in this respect, i welcome the rapporteur's call to consider immigration as a positive element of the european population, but above all to strengthen european policies in the field of social integration of migrants, the fight against discrimination and xenophobia. in conclusion, i would like to stress the need to mobilise public policies at all levels necessary for the successful implementation of the objectives mentioned. local and regional authorities have a key role to play in this respect and must be constantly involved.
in writing. the demographic strategy of the european union addresses many social and economic issues. i would like to stress, however, the importance of a coherent policy for young people, particularly as regards access to the labour market. it is well known that the 25-30 age group is present in a relatively small proportion on the european labour market compared to other categories of the population. the european commission and the member states should increase the number of legislative initiatives and pilot programmes that lead to easier access to employment for young people. examples of such initiatives could be: giving tax incentives to firms that hire young people or broadening the range of flexible employment contracts. secondly, we are faced, particularly in the new member states, with the problem of regions being left behind by young people in large numbers. the european union's cohesion policy should, through the structural funds it makes available to the member states, create favourable conditions for young people to develop their professional and business projects in their communities of origin. member states must complement eu financial support with measures such as priority access for young people to land and housing, tax incentives for young entrepreneurs or access to low-interest loans for youth projects.

in writing. harmonising the actions taken by member states, airports and airlines to ensure civil aviation security is a pressing need to respond to terrorist threats. however, a balance must be struck between efforts to enhance safety and ensure the comfort of air transport users. every effort should be made, in particular, to improve the technical performance of screening equipment and to apply the single control for transit flights, which allows both a reduction in processing time and, in the medium and long term, an effective reduction in real costs. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the measures in question are necessary to ensure the safety of the union industry. the financing aspects need to be clarified as soon as possible so that both eu taxpayers and transport users have a real picture of the destination of the amounts collected, clearly separating the financing of direct measures from the costs of insurance and any state aid for additional security measures that a member state may impose.

i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur on her work and on the effort she has made to find a compromise on this extremely sensitive subject. as a member of the european parliament from a new member state, i consider the 2% increase to be beneficial, even though we would have liked a significantly higher percentage, especially for member states with both low milk quotas and untapped production potential. the increase in national milk quotas does not constitute a threat to the stability of the milk market. i would like to draw attention to the fact that a 2% increase in quotas will actually result in an increase in milk production at community level of only 0.8%. i also believe that we need to maintain the current quota system to stimulate the consolidation of existing farms and encourage the creation of new ones. the terms used in relation to quotas in the context of the reform of the common agricultural policy are those of the 'soft landing' procedure, i.e. the gradual abandonment of quotas. the new member states, and in particular romania and bulgaria, which only joined on 1 january 2007 and which, using the same language, 'take off' abruptly, will have difficulties in adapting their 'take-off' procedures to those for 'landing' smoothly. if this proposal had not been accepted, the quota allocated to romania would have been exhausted, as in 2007, by the middle of the year, which does not stimulate, but completely discourages the development projects of our farmers. i hope the vote on this report in the house will be as strong as the vote in the committee on agriculture.
in writing. mrs jeggle's report is extremely important not only for proposals to increase milk quotas but also for defining principles that we need to take into account when we consider agricultural policy as a whole. following discussions in the committee on agriculture and rural development, we agreed that an increase in milk quotas for member states is necessary as from 1 april 2008. i represent romania in the ep, a new member state which has been facing a crisis of milk quotas since the first year of accession, which is insufficient to meet market demand and is not in line with current realities. the romanian milk sector has made great progress since the negotiation of the milk quota in 2004 and up to accession, through investments in modern technology, the expansion of production capacities and the recruitment of new staff. maintaining a milk quota at that level would mean bankruptcy for investors, unemployment in rural areas specialised in milk production and processing and an increase in imports and the price paid by consumers. the report is a turning point because the european union is showing flexibility in tackling a problem facing several member states. finally, the beneficiaries of this report are the citizens of europe.
as vice-president of envi, i would like to make a few remarks on the impact of climate change on agriculture. in recent years, intensive farming has made farmers a major contributor to global warming, and today they are fighting its devastating effects. statistics estimate that agriculture is responsible for 17 to 32 percent of greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. agriculture continues to be polluting as a result of the unreasonable use of fertilisers, the improper storage of animal manure, the unreasonable use of land, and i am referring in particular to deforestation and overgrazing. global warming is irreversible, and the frequent occurrence of droughts or floods in the future should not surprise us. i therefore support the idea put forward in the report of creating a safety net at european level to support eu farmers in the event of an ecological, climatic or epidemiological disaster. in this context, i call on the european commission to examine the possibility of setting up urgently a fund or a multi-risk insurance mechanism, which would be aimed at eu farmers and be financed both from the eu budget and from the member states' budgets.
the common agricultural policy is one of the basic pillars of the european construction, and the debate on how to improve this policy should be a constant not only for the european institutions but also within the member states in the constituencies where we have been elected. i am glad that the commission communication and the report drawn up by mr goepel identify some solutions to make the common agricultural policy more effective so that farmers and the rural population can be confident that this policy is for their benefit and not a set of bureaucratic provisions drawn up in some brussels office. but we must ensure that the proposals of the commission, the council and ourselves are sufficiently flexible and grounded in reality to be able to measure their effectiveness when they are put into practice. romania, the country i represent in the european parliament, has 25% of its workforce in agriculture and 40% of the total population lives in rural areas. these are figures that demonstrate the importance of agriculture and the rural environment for romania and for our economy. the solutions we find for cap reform must take into account cases like romania's, with a very large agricultural sector and in the process of modernisation.
i am pleased to take the floor on a reality that is so often ignored, namely the situation of rural women. although the system of laws and regulations applicable at the level of the union and at the level of each member state excludes any discrimination, it is clear that there is a huge gap between the life of women in urban areas and that of women in rural areas. romania, like other new eu member states, is in a much worse situation than the overall one described in the report. in the 1990s, with the decline of industry, a phenomenon emerged that western european countries had not experienced before: migration from the city to the countryside as a way of economic survival. in our region, rural poverty has affected and continues to affect predominantly women, making them the most vulnerable victims of trafficking in human beings. unfortunately, industrial agriculture, which could have absorbed some of the female workforce from the countryside, has also experienced a phenomenon of disruption. public services in health, education, transport, water and sanitation have deteriorated rapidly, with many of the eu's less developed countries' villages virtually lacking such services. rural women, especially young and middle-aged women, could develop independent economic activities if they had access to bank loans, and i think we can consider the possibility of establishing a bank to provide micro-loans in rural areas.
in 2006, in the european union, the ratio of the income of the top 20 percent of the population to the bottom 20 percent was 4.8. unfortunately, in portugal, lithuania and latvia, the ratio was over 6. it is clear that rural people have lower incomes than urban people, and this is even more evident for women. improving the situation of women in rural areas requires the efficient use of structural funds. the development of transport infrastructure, education, health services, communication infrastructure and information technology and the service sector in rural areas will lead to their economic development and, by implication, to the improvement of the situation of rural women. i conclude by saying that rural areas can, through investment, transform the land available into industrial parks that provide jobs. efficient transport infrastructure allows distance to be measured in time rather than kilometres, so that those working in urban areas can live in rural areas, thus contributing to their economic development.
the success of the lisbon strategy requires sustained economic growth in both urban and rural areas of the european union, and women play a crucial role in the development of these areas. i therefore welcome the report which analyses the situation of rural women and makes concrete recommendations to improve their situation in the context of globalisation and the achievement of the lisbon objectives. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. it's about education. the statistics available to us show that a small number of rural women have access to higher education because of financial difficulties and the poor quality of education in these areas. rural women must have improved access to education and continuing training and opportunities to reconcile family and professional life. this is a key element that should be strengthened with the active role of women in political life and the socio-economic development of rural areas.
ladies and gentlemen, since we are discussing a subject which is not only about equal opportunities but also about rural development in general, i shall refer to the measures which apply at community level in this field. the programmes and funds in pillar 2 of rural development have a much higher percentage of resources than the european union's special programmes for equal opportunities. if we can make it easier for women to access programmes like leader, dedicated to rural development, we will have much more to gain than if we use only the resources of the equal, progress or daphne programmes. within the eu budget, rural development funds amount to 11%, while the entire citizenship chapter, which includes equal opportunities programmes, is less than 1%. this is the european union's great challenge in this case: to be able to communicate, to mobilise and to facilitate the link between european funds and the various projects that can be initiated in rural areas by women.
in writing. the eu is facing major social changes, which have brought with them issues of migration, social security and poverty. eu programmes have made an important contribution to improving the situation of rural women. however, women are not involved in decision-making in the communities they live in. as a worrying case in point, the majority of women in rural romania have incomes of less than 5 euro/day, and a third do not use any means of information. consider three priority areas of action for achieving equal opportunities and improving the situation of rural women:- improving economic status by supporting women's access to new earning and property opportunities; - full involvement of women in decision-making and enhanced capacity to change/influence decisions that directly affect them; - access of rural women to essential services (health, education) and infrastructure. member states must define public policies to encourage women's participation in the labour market, in decision-making and in combating all forms of discrimination.
at the current level of oil, biogas is an energy resource that needs to be taken into account, especially in the context of the european union's increasing dependence on hydrocarbon imports. we all know it, the target of 20% renewable energy in total european energy consumption by 2020 is well known. or, in these circumstances, it is obvious that biogas will also have to be stimulated, especially through financial instruments, as an energy resource. biogas and other biofuels, together with solar and wind energy, can significantly reduce dependence on conventional energy sources. in addition, compared to other types of renewables, biogas has the advantage that it can be used for both electricity and heat production, as well as for transport. perhaps a new biogas directive alone would be too much, but i think it is welcome that the commission should be asked to present a special report on biogas in the european union, which should also contain recommendations on european and national legislation in this area.

on behalf of the pse group. without policies to encourage a rise in births and child-rearing and care facilities, the proportion of the population aged over 65 will increase from 20% to 28% by 2025. the elderly have special needs, and society must change to meet them. adapted housing, health care and elderly care services are needed. in this context, the role of ict is becoming increasingly important. digital television, mobile phones, computers and even the internet are already used by some older people. many of them communicate with their children in other countries via the internet and webcams, whether in rural or urban settings. however, the percentage of european citizens aged over 65 using the internet is only 10%. it is worth noting that over 21% of european citizens over 50 have severe hearing, vision or dexterity problems, making it difficult for them to use standard ict equipment. in june 2007, the commission called on member states and industry to help implement the action plan 'integrating older people in the information society'. in this context, the home awareness support programme, to be carried out under the 7th framework research programme, will have a budget of €150 million from the community budget, with member states spending at least €150 million over the period 2008-2013, of course the participating member states. the objectives of this programme are: to promote the development of innovative ict-based products, services and systems for older people; to create a critical mass of european-specific research, development and innovation in technologies and services for older people in the information society; to improve the conditions for exploitation of research results by businesses. any member state may participate in this programme. two years after the start of the programme, the commission will produce an interim report and in 2013 will produce a final evaluation of the programme. i think the elderly deserve a chance, we have this duty! according to statistics, the number of older people in europe will increase by 40% between 2010 and 2030. this presents challenges but also opportunities for public policy and the european future. a truly prosperous and competitive europe must find the right answer to these challenges and fully exploit the potential of new demographic trends. the elderly european citizen must benefit from quality services and conditions, and his or her experience must be used for the continuous development of society. in the context of the european union's aspiration to become an information-based economy and society, information technologies are an innovative response to this situation and the involvement of the european community in the relevant programmes is more than necessary. i would like to highlight two important aspects of the use of new technologies to improve the quality of life of older people. first, the european citizen must be trained and informed about the new technological possibilities offered. older people, especially in the new member states, are not familiar with this area at all or only partially, and the resulting losses for society as a whole are evident. the success of the decision discussed today therefore depends largely on europe's capacity to mobilise for their education and information. secondly, particular attention should be paid to women, whose share in the ageing society is higher than that of men, due to their longer life expectancy. this element must be taken into account both in scientific research into the ageing process and in the practical implementation of public policies. finally, i reiterate the importance of focusing on the situation in the new member states, where older people are less well off. the low standard of living, combined with a lack of knowledge of the use of new technologies, makes this category a priority target for future efforts at european level.
the exclusion of older people from the benefits of information technology in society is problematic, especially as the proportion of the european population aged 65 to 80 will soon reach 40%. the joint research and development programme, to which the european union will be associated, is therefore welcome, with a view to improving the lives of these people. what i want to stress, however, is that the community's financial involvement in the project is limited. the community contribution is capped at eur 150 million, provided that it comes from the budget of the r & d framework programme, which totals over eur 50 billion. moreover, the community contribution cannot exceed 50% of the public funds used in the project, an atypically small percentage for a project of such importance. beyond the concrete benefits that the it solutions identified through this programme will bring to older people, the union's participation in the project is a very good opportunity to contribute to the quality of life of europeans and for this reason the community financial contribution should exceed the national amounts allocated to this type of research.

education or health are not real priorities. yet we know that women's health and education are key to development. all this is at the heart of the communication on gender equality in development cooperation adopted by the european commission on 8 march 2007. this policy is a response to the commitments made in the european consensus on development on gender equality in all our cooperation policies and practices. the ambition of this communication is to develop a european vision and harmonised support for the promotion of gender equality in all regions and all developing countries. the communication also serves as a guide for new aid modalities, including budget support. contrary to the criticisms in your report, i believe that budget support provides new opportunities to support gender equality effectively. why would you do that? i have often had occasion to mention the reasons why i was in favour of budget support wherever possible. budget support gives us an incomparably stronger lever in the political dialogue with the authorities of the partner country. it gives us the opportunity to discuss, for example, policy options, and among other things also the need to develop better the potential of women in the economic and social development of a country. furthermore, we base our support in this case on verification of tangible outcomes presented or revealed by indicators that are always disaggregated by gender, and thus clearly show gender gaps where they exist. the objectives by which a country's performance is measured are aligned with the millennium development goals and, for the most part, are highly relevant to improving women's living conditions. the aim is to increase the rate of girls' schooling and the number of prenatal consultations, to name just a few. and it is on the basis of the progress made by a country on these kinds of objectives that the european commission disburses its variable budget support tranches. in the course of this debate, someone spoke about conditionality. when you give budgetary support, you obviously have the possibility, in some way, of obliging the partner to respect criteria, to respect conditionalities. it's much stronger in terms of positive influence than when you don't do budget support. i think that, in any case, i am prepared to continue this debate in other contexts. but i am firmly convinced, from my own experience today, that budgetary aid, where possible, is obviously much more effective. for a long time, we have taken a two-pronged approach. on the one hand, we integrate gender equality into all our policies and actions, such as budget support and policy dialogue with our partners. this requires, among other things, the training of our colleagues in the gender delegations. thus, since 2004, more than a thousand colleagues have received gender-specific training and we have now set up a gender helpdesk to continue this training in the future. we also finance specific actions to promote gender equality. such actions are included in some national indicative programmes, but more importantly there are thematic programmes which complement geographical cooperation. the programmes 'investing in human resources' and 'human rights and democracy' incorporate specific elements for the promotion of gender equality. the investing in human resources programme has €57 million for gender-specific actions between 2007 and 2013, an average annual amount almost three times what we did until 2006. of course, gender equality is also integrated into the other thematic programmes, whether in education, health, agriculture, the environment or culture. it is true that there is still a long way to go, but i am convinced that with a common commitment to promoting equality between women and men, in collaboration especially with women in developing countries, we will be able to fight poverty and build more just societies.
reporting for the opinion of the committee on women's rights and gender equality. - ladies and gentlemen, i see that the report has already generated reactions. hopefully, it's a proof of his political relevance. the commission's communication was a very good starting point, and parliament added useful clarifications. i would like to explain the principle that i started with in constructing the position. the goal was clear, we support women's empowerment in development cooperation. there is, beyond the equality reasons, ample evidence that women are a good investment, excellent multipliers of results. but how do we get the most efficiency in achieving the goal? we could have asked the beneficiary states for strict criteria on women's empowerment. they already exist, anyway. however, we can also expect weaker reactions, lack of expertise and administrative capacity, formal commitments in strategic development plans and lack of practical implementation of these commitments. failure to comply with the obligations may result in the reduction or suspension of the aid itself. it would hurt the bottom line, it would make women pay for the inefficiency of governments, which we don't want. under these circumstances, we have chosen to insist on the fulfillment of those requirements over which we have both control and the means of action. we therefore call on the commission and the member states to ensure coherence between other community policies and development policy. otherwise, some aspects of the external trade policy or the common agricultural policy may interfere negatively with our objectives. given the significant differences in the gender dimension of member states' policies, we believe that the implementation of the european commission's roadmap on gender equality within the union is a necessary precondition for a real and effective empowerment of women in development cooperation, a policy largely managed by member states. new forms of aid seem to have weakened the focus on women. we call for an assessment of their gender impact and appropriate corrective measures, in the context of accountability and transparency of the spending of funds we have towards european citizens.

on behalf of the ppe-de group. our institution's budgetary guidelines for 2009 are the basis for the european parliament's budget this autumn. but beyond the amounts and programmes, this year's budgetary guidelines also address a matter which i consider very important: the legal situation of assistants in the european parliament. i want to thank mr. lewandowski for bringing this up. i believe it is time that the old system became clearer and more transparent and ensured for all these young people the same social and tax rights as the other members of the staff of the institution. for these there are the staff regulations of the european communities, a very comprehensive document which ensures that staff working in the institutions of the european union have adequate social protection. parliamentary assistants are also, for the most part, citizens of a country other than the one in which they work and should therefore enjoy the protection afforded to all workers in international organisations. i do not consider it normal that there should be cases in which assistants are subject to additional tax obligations by the belgian state, since they pay all their taxes and social security contributions in the state of their nationality. but parliament needs clear rules for assistants also in situations such as illness or maternity. in several resolutions, the european parliament has already asked the secretary-general and the working party on the status of assistants and the pension fund to draft a new set of rules to address the problems facing assistants at the moment. i believe it is our responsibility to the european citizens that there should be only clear and transparent rules within this institution.
the establishment of the climate change commission was driven by the direct impact that climate change has on the planet, threatening the existence of humanity as a whole. we are discussing the european treaty, we want to strengthen the community institutions, we are making plans for the future. we have to be very careful, because we may not have to. our health, our economy, our ecosystems, our way of life, europe as we know it is in great danger. the scientists have made their position known, and i have agreed with them overwhelmingly. the studies are very clear and we can see here in brussels how on one day the weather phenomena of all four seasons occur, which is clearly not normal. the mandate of the climate change commission is very clear: it must analyse the current situation, take stock of the prospects for combating climate change and make concrete proposals for eu policy in this area at all levels of decision-making. today's resolution contains a very large number of proposals for action by the commission. however, in order to have an effect, i believe that these proposals should be further developed and possibly included in the commission's final report, together with suggestions for the timing of their practical implementation. moreover, it is imperative that the european institutions propose as soon as possible a clear strategy to be negotiated internationally. it is useless to take action in europe alone. we need to be the global climate change advocates. only concrete measures, which take account only of the arguments relating to the stability of citizens' lives, can mitigate the effects of climate change, and these measures must be implemented in the shortest possible time.
climate change is becoming more and more evident and humanity needs to change its behaviour, paying more attention to environmental protection. europe is already experiencing very hot summers, with periods of drought followed by heavy rains and flooding, violent storms, desertification of vast areas, particularly in the southern and eastern areas. romania has not been spared the effects of climate change. in recent years, we've had devastating floods, heat waves, violent storms, desertification in the southern and eastern regions, decreased rainfall. all of this has resulted in loss of life, extensive damage to property, and a decline in agricultural production. europe must act decisively today to reduce the effects of climate change. europe must take action to improve water management, flood protection, wastewater treatment, coastal protection, energy efficiency, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, cleaner agriculture, cleaner transport and forestry. special attention should be paid to areas that are becoming desertified. europe should consider investing in an irrigation system that supports member states at risk of declining agricultural production as a result of desertification to build or improve their irrigation systems. i congratulate the commission on the green paper on a new urban mobility policy. 20% of european motorists could use public transport. reducing the speed limit will also help to combat the greenhouse effect. the introduction of aviation into the emissions trading scheme is a step forward. the inclusion of shipping in this scheme is now being considered. unfortunately, the current union budget does not sufficiently and coherently integrate the actions needed to mitigate climate change. the climate change budget is modest.
in writing. − as head of the romanian socialist delegation, i would like to explain the delegation's negative vote on the resolution on tibet. in fact, the resolution is not defending human rights and we cannot accept that human rights fall hostage to geopolitical agendas and interests. it is lenient with respect to human rights and hypocritical, because it is forceful in proposing political solutions that do not take into account the realities in china. through this resolution, the eu is losing its credibility, promoting in reality, behind its statements of support for human rights, a dangerous agenda of "political autonomy" and independence for tibet, in clear contradiction to the "one-china policy" principle. at the same time, the eu is losing its encouraging influence on china in the process of opening. consequently, the resolution stands for the partition of china and not for the support and promotion of human rights, which are being used as a pretext for pushing forward different geopolitical agendas.
mr president, a few weeks ago, together with mr von wogau, the chairman of the subcommittee on security and defence, i visited the eubam mission in odessa, ukraine. its mandate is to help ukraine and moldova manage their common border better, by providing both expertise and support. once there, we could see that the mission, through the quality and professionalism of its people, has managed to build a solid reputation of professional authority useful not only in passing on expertise to its counterparts, but also in mediating between them on important questions of mutual interest. moreover, by flying the eu flag as the only embodiment of our union in that large and important area, the eubam mission is a very efficient ambassador for our institutions, thus contributing to the concrete implementation of both our security strategy and our neighbourhood policy there. it has most certainly set an example worthy of being applied in other areas of interest to us.
in april, bucharest was for the first time presented in all media channels only in a favorable light, on the occasion of the nato summit held in romania. many did not believe that our country could organize a summit of such a magnitude: 3000 officials from 49 countries, 3500 journalists, the bucharest summit with the largest participation and the most complex agenda in nato history. i would like to highlight three major conclusions of the summit: croatia and albania have been invited to join nato; nato will install an anti-missile system complementary to the us shield - this shield will protect nato states not covered by the us shield; nato leaders have committed to increasing their forces in afghanistan to fight the taliban, to share the burden of military operations and to limit restrictions on the use of their troops.
deforestation has reached an alarming global rate of 13 million hectares a year. the phenomenon is closely correlated with excessive deforestation and illegal trade in wood products. we could continue to turn a blind eye to the slaughter of forests, assuming that we europeans have efficient systems for protecting biodiversity and consumers. in the eu, about 50 per cent of timber imports from tropical countries and 20 per cent of timber imports from eastern europe and the russian federation come from illegal sources. so we are contributing to the illegal deforestation in the amazon, and moreover, the phenomenon is also widespread in eu member states such as estonia, romania and bulgaria. we must have a consistent and honest approach to the problem of illegal logging and trafficking both in third countries and, above all, in the union. i therefore ask the european commission to submit without delay a legislative proposal that only legally verified wood and wood products can be marketed on the european market. i have therefore put a written statement to the ep and i encourage my colleagues to join us in the fight against illegal logging.
to make the most of the opportunities offered by globalisation, the union needs to modernise its social policies and invest heavily in human resources. since the 1990s, social protection spending has remained around 28% of gross domestic product. between 2000 and 2007, the number of jobs increased by 13 million, while the unemployment rate fell from 9% to 7%. at the same time, some 80 million european citizens are living below the poverty line. the risk of child poverty is 19% in the european union. the lisbon treaty underlines the importance of the union having a social market economy. social changes taking place in the context of globalisation relate to unemployment, pension reform, tax reform, poverty reduction and investment in education and childcare. education can play a vital role in compensating for socioeconomic disadvantage and in opening the way for the successful development of the child. member states also need to improve their health systems and tackle poverty among the elderly.

in writing. i would like to highlight a few aspects of the article which reaffirms the importance of the principle of solidarity in this report. cohesion policy still accounts for around one third of the european union's annual budget. however, we cannot fail to note that this area is becoming less and less important in relation to the increases in competitiveness policy for growth and employment. for example, compared to 2007, budget line 1a - for competitiveness - increased by 18.4%, while 1b - covering the area of cohesion - increased by only 3.1%. in addition, we must take into account the effects of the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon on cohesion policy. the structural funds - which are currently non-compulsory expenditure and on which parliament has the final say in the budgetary procedure - will be the subject of a joint decision by the council of ministers and parliament. however, it is known that each year the council makes substantial cuts in the european sums devoted to cohesion policy. i therefore believe it is important to achieve the objectives of the lisbon strategy, without neglecting the disparities that still exist between european regions.
in writing. support for the european parliament's motion for a resolution on eu policy actions on organ donation and transplantation. i call on the european commission to propose a more comprehensive directive setting out the quality and safety requirements for the donation and transport of organs for transplantation in the european union. this directive would also provide for ways of preventing possible abuses. the new legislation will have to complement and strengthen the efforts of the member states to improve the current situation by imposing guidelines at european level, taking account of medical advances. i insist on the involvement of member states, including my home member state, romania, in educating citizens by presenting the benefits of organ donation and raising awareness that organ donation and transplantation means lives saved. i also support the involvement of the european commission in organising public debates with relevant european non-governmental organisations to identify the best solutions, both in terms of the communication campaign and the exploitation of the experience and good practices of the member states. speed of reaction in such cases is essential. better organization of the national health system is needed, as well as increased awareness among paramedics of such emergencies.
in writing. the shortage of organs that has led to the rapid development of commercialisation and transplant tourism is a major health problem facing the european union. organ trafficking is caused by a combination of factors such as poverty, corruption, or crime, which is why eastern european countries are the most exposed to this phenomenon. to prevent this 'transplant tourism', the environment committee report calls for organ donation to be done altruistically and voluntarily, without it becoming a source of profit for the donors. member states should take measures to protect the poorest and most vulnerable donors from becoming victims of organ trafficking. however, there are considerable differences between eu countries in the way donation and transplantation is organised, the donor community and the sources of organ harvesting. for example, the low number of donors in romania is due to the lack of an effective donor identification system and doctors trained to coordinate the organization of a transplant. because of this, the european average for the number of donors is 20, and in romania it is only 0.5. we need the right technical and logistical infrastructure, as well as psychological and organisational support to reduce the gap between supply and demand.
