, in writing. mountain regions are important in the geographical structure of the european union, being an area where traditions, culture and language are preserved in perhaps the best conditions compared to other areas in the territory of the 27 member states. unfortunately, national governments are not currently implementing integrated regional development strategies, and there are many disparities in this respect, which are slowly but surely contributing to the depopulation of these regions. in line with the union's slogan 'unity in diversity', i welcome the parliament's decision to ask the european commission to draw up an integrated strategy for the sustainable development and use of resources in mountain areas, which can offer equal opportunities to european citizens who have chosen to live in the more difficult conditions of mountain areas. given that there are now discussions on decoupling compensatory payments in mountain areas, i believe that it is our duty as members of the european parliament to support the maintenance of existing financial support for mountain areas for the future. the mountain will thus be able to become a protected area, capable of sustainable development and a true oasis for european and international tourists.
in writing. the country i represent - romania - is covered by a third of mountains, and people living in mountainous areas are disadvantaged compared to other categories of rural dwellers. the proposals contained in the ebner report are welcome and i am convinced that a coherent european union strategy for mountain areas - which is essential and urgent - would make a major contribution to raising the standard of living in these areas. at the same time, i would stress that better regulation of community funds for rural development is equally urgently needed. for example, the romanian authorities have launched programmes to support micro-enterprises and tourism, funded by the eafrd. small businesses and guesthouses are particularly important for the revitalization of mountain areas. the applicant's guidelines for these measures, which require complex formalities, were published only one day before the opening of the session, although they had been drawn up as early as august. this is a clear breach of the principle of ensuring that potential beneficiaries are informed in a fair and transparent manner. i believe that community legislation should impose measures to avoid such situations, which render the union's financial effort useless.
in writing. we welcome the report by mr ebner. the mountainous area of romania covers 33% of the country's surface. as in other european countries, the mountain area is at risk of depopulation and the reduction of the economic activities specific to these areas. we need an integrated european strategy for the sustainable development of the mountain area. we call for a strong emphasis on supporting agriculture, organic products, agro-tourism and access and communications in the mountain area. we also support the encouragement of young families to set up family-type agro-tourism farms, so that the mountain area becomes an area of economic interest again.
cooperation between the european union institutions in the fight against terrorism must work well in the face of the increase in this phenomenon. terrorism has become the principal enemy of world stability and peace. if we look back at the events of september 11 or the events in madrid and london a few years ago, we have the perfect configuration of a painting that expresses horror, fear and suffering. in order to ensure the security of our citizens, we must take urgent action in the field of counter-terrorism. they should be carried out in close cooperation with local and regional authorities. nothing in the framework decision may be interpreted as reducing or restricting fundamental rights or freedoms, such as freedom of expression, assembly or association. the expression of radical, polemical or controversial opinions in a public debate on sensitive political issues, including terrorism, does not fall within the scope of the framework decision. as long as we maintain a balance between respecting the freedoms and protecting the security of our citizens, any initiative is welcome.
in the third millennium, the beauty of the global village has been overtaken by the threat of global terrorism. since states, in the name of subsidiarity, can only control 10-15% of cyberspace, leaving the rest to the private domain and families, we believe that for the first time, a global partnership approach is required, and that global terrorism should be responded to with a new concept - "global take care of the global village". the european union will thus demonstrate a concern for planetary security, as well as a concern for itself, through a different approach and a strategy to protect global cyberspace.
mr president, in spite of its horrible consequences, international terrorism is still, sadly, a controversial subject. we want protection, but we protest at the cost and distress to authorities when they propose to implement measures to that effect. we deplore the terrorist attacks, but we protest at the limitations to the full exercise of our rights, in spite of the fact that we know very well that the perpetrators are abusing our democratic system. ideally any limitation of our rights should be compensated by a corresponding increase in our security in the face of terrorist attacks. equally, we tend to resist legislative uniformisation against terrorism, although we know that the consequences are similarly destructive. furthermore, attacks might increase in frequency when the punishment is milder. therefore, to have an effective protection against terrorism, perhaps we should make up our minds and reconcile first these conflicting views.
i mean the report of mrs. roure. the right to the protection of personal data is a fundamental right. citizens whose data is processed have rights that must be respected at both national and european level. at european level, there are many regulations and directives requiring the exchange of information on crimes committed by european citizens in a member state other than the one of residence. i am referring to the regulation on access to the occupation of road haulage operator, the directive on the facilitation of the crossborder application of road safety rules. all these european regulations require the creation of computer systems to enable notifications and related information to be transmitted between member states. all the associated computer systems must contain a public part, but also a secure part containing data on offences committed in other member states, which must be accessed only by the responsible institutions and, above all, with respect for and protection of personal data.

in writing. ensuring a legal framework for the protection of personal data within the eu's third pillar has been a concern of all eu presidencies in recent years. however, the framework decision adopted in 2006 was more of a compromise solution, which merely agreed on the lowest common denominator on personal data protection. for this reason, a further consultation of the european parliament on the extension of the scope of the framework decision and an analysis of its impact on fundamental rights within the union can only be welcomed. the main objective of the amendments should be to ensure a level of data protection similar to that in the first column and, in this respect, i regret that the commission's initial proposal was amended by the council. it is also regrettable that the provision on the working group with national data protection authorities has been removed by the council, which is a step backwards in the process of creating an effective system of personal data protection.
in writing. effective protection of personal data remains a prerequisite of modern democracy. while this protection may in some cases involve the alteration of community personal data bases so that the details of personal or material circumstances no longer allow them to be attributed to an identifiable natural person, we must be aware that the management of this global system for storing and processing information requires the existence of a particularly high-performance associated security system. since real security cannot be guaranteed by our adherence to a set of common principles, i believe that a pragmatic analysis of the risks involved in police and judicial cooperation between states with different levels of expertise in the field is necessary. to be very clear, i want to reiterate here the need for newly integrated states to benefit from a rapid transfer of expertise in the field so that the overall security of the system is not in any way affected.
in writing. with the expansion of the scope of terrorism to cyberspace, with the possibility of manipulating the masses much faster and with fairly low possibilities of rapid identification of the real perpetrators of terrorist acts, we consider that such a decision is welcome, in the context of the protection of the civil rights and freedoms of every citizen, but also the creation of the appropriate framework for the rapid identification and resolution of criminal cases, especially those that threaten the security of people, states, national infrastructures. we welcome the decision to consider the objectives set out in the framework decision of major european interest, in particular as regards common rules for the protection of personal data, so that the same principles and rules can be applied at member state level. i also think that a recommendation should be made on the classification of information in accordance with international classification systems, so that there are no longer any differences between member states and others in the application of security measures. two basic strategies must be considered in ensuring data protection and security systems: everything that is not prohibited is allowed, everything that is not allowed is prohibited.

in writing. − i voted in favour of the bologna process and student mobility report for several reasons: the bologna process at eu level has been one of the most revolutionary elements in the global education and training market. the job market was not ready for such a change either. it is not yet fully receptive to the three-cycle education system, 3-2-3 (bachelor, master, doctorate years) but, on the other hand, in many cases, before the introduction of the new system, organizations employed students from the bachelor cycle already during their studies. another progressive element was student mobility through european schools and the system of common diplomas, facilitated in particular by the european credit transfer system (ects). the trend among the world's great universities to move students from one course of study to another in various locations around the globe, especially where they have long-standing branches, shows that these have been real successes. the proposal made by ecvet (european credit system for vocational education and training) to transfer, recognise and accumulate learning outcomes acquired by individuals in formal, non-formal and informal contexts for the purpose of qualification, without focusing on time spent on accumulating knowledge, skills and competences, is also revolutionary. this trend is also global.

in writing. − the lack of statistical data on waste generation and management prevents the european union from implementing a harmonised waste policy. statistical tools are necessary to assess compliance with the principle of preventing environmental degradation due to the use of waste and monitoring it at the time of its production, collection and disposal. member states have recognised that there are insufficient statistical data and that the definitions contained in this regulation are not sufficient to achieve comparable results between member states. therefore, data collection can be better achieved at community level in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. as regards statistics from agriculture, fisheries and forestry, it is necessary to consider to what extent the treatment of agricultural waste and organic waste will be covered by this regulation. there are therefore a number of key points which require greater attention in order to ensure a high level of data accuracy and, consequently, harmonisation of statistical information at community level.

the third maritime package has emerged from the erika and prestige accidents, to which are added the accidents in the black sea in december 2007 and even the accident in the port of taragona this month. these accidents have caused immense damage both to coastal areas and to the marine environment. the package covers maritime traffic monitoring, maritime accident investigation, liability of carriers of passengers by sea in the event of accidents, port state control, common rules and standards for organisations with a role in the inspection and control of ships. i would like to point out that the new form of the paris memorandum entered into force on 17 september 2008. it is essential that all ships calling at european ports comply with certain security standards. i would remind you that the black and grey lists, published on 18 june 2008 on the paris memorandum website, list one and six member states respectively. a quarter of the member states therefore need to improve the security of their flagged vessels. regardless of the technical condition, a vessel in distress shall have access to a specially equipped place of refuge. european ports must be equipped with this facility and port administrations must be able to recover the costs incurred for the stationing of the vessel and the remediation of its deficiencies. i also believe that the liability of shipowners for the carriage of passengers should apply accordingly to inland waters. i want to congratulate my colleagues who worked and negotiated this maritime package. i believe that it is of vital importance for the economic future of the european union.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think this debate has been very fruitful, because it has certainly shown the willingness of parliament, the commission and the council to work together to address and give answers to the european citizens on a phenomenon which is becoming increasingly worrying, namely piracy. the debate has produced, and i share this analysis, the following: i do not think we should dwell too much on questions of competence, whether it be the european union or nato, we cannot waste time. i believe that we must strengthen coordination, but we have a duty to intervene in the meantime to prevent the strengthening of the position of the pirate organisations. at the same time, it is important to take action to prevent and eradicate the possible causes that lead to the growth of the phenomenon and the recruitment of pirates. it is clear that in areas where poverty is very high, pirate organizations have an easy time recruiting, especially young people, who are ready to do anything and to join these paramilitary organizations. that is why, alongside the control and repression measures which must be taken by the countries of the european union - and i am glad that they have already been taken - we must take action - and here the commission has an important role to play - to help some developing countries to grow economically, to prevent poverty from becoming a tool which facilitates piracy. we must also work to understand - and here too the commission can play an extremely important role in understanding - what is behind piracy, what are the links with fundamentalism, with terrorism; what are the strengths, what are the reasons. the commission can also give an important hand to the other european institutions in this area. we cannot simply stand by and watch, we cannot wait, and certainly not with parliament's strong action, which is pushing the council and the commission to act, we must ensure the safety of seafarers, we must ensure the safety of goods coming from outside the european union and supplying the european union, we must ensure that the problem is not just - it is right to raise it not only in the seas closest to the european union - where there are also fishermen who are working, and mr fraga stressed with concern that incidents are happening even closer. we must also look at what is happening in other parts of the world, because piracy is also affecting ships flying the flags of european union countries in very distant seas. that is why we must not waste any more time, but i think that today the european union's will has clearly emerged, particularly the council's, with the support of the commission, to intervene and to continue to act firmly to prevent and, i believe, with strategic plans to prevent the intensification of terrorist action. that is why the council will find the commission's support in all initiatives to combat terrorism and also to prevent it, terrorism linked to piracy, to prevent it and to counter it. so i believe that by this cooperation, with parliament's watchful eye, some positive results can be achieved. on the defence side, i too agree with minister bussereau's assessment of the words of our friend general morillon: it is a matter of defending the interests, but also the values of the european union.
president of the council. - mr president, i would first like to express my deepest sympathy with the shooting which claimed ten lives in the finnish high school in kauhajoki and my sincere condolences to the families of the victims and to the finnish members of parliament who are present in this house or who are called upon to do their work. in reply to mrs ticǎu's question, i would like to point out that at its meeting on 13 june 2008 the council reached political agreement on the three proposals forming part of the 'road transport' package. the aim of these new texts is to harmonise national regulations which may differ and thus be a source of legal uncertainty for road hauliers. the main substantive changes are: a more precise definition of the concept of 'cabotage', a standardised presentation of the community licence, the conforming copies and the driver attestation, the strengthening of the provisions obliging a member state to take measures when a carrier commits an infringement in another member state, and finally a better link between national registers of infringements in order to ensure european monitoring of road hauliers. the european parliament adopted the reports on this package at first reading at its meeting on 20 may. the work now has to be concentrated on reaching a compromise between the council and parliament. given the translation delays, work on the texts of the respective common positions could not begin until the end of august and the council hopes to be able to adopt the common positions on the three proposals in the coming weeks and to forward them, mr president, to the european parliament as soon as possible.

european schools are recognised in europe as elite schools providing a solid education for young people. in 1953, jean monnet said that the aim of these schools was to bring together children from europe, regardless of nationality, and to instill in them the spirit and the european identity so that they could then give birth to a united and prosperous europe. the following important aspects must be taken into account in the reform programme for these schools. all 23 official languages of the european union must be present in these schools and children must have the opportunity to speak their mother tongue. unfortunately, there are still official languages of the european union that are not spoken in any european school. in addition, one of the objectives of the european schools is to give unity to groups of children, to bring them together and to facilitate the development of a spirit of tolerance and communication between them. so i don't think it's appropriate to divide them into those three categories. the latter, and others, as it is called, are allowed to study at such a school only within the limits of the places left after their occupation by the children of european officials. this categorization is discriminatory and i propose to remove it from the statute of european schools.

european policies related to the reform of traditional schools in their becoming european schools, involving local administrations up to national ones, mean, in our opinion, three types of reforms to be carried out: a systemic reform, including curricular, based on quality and efficiency, a continuous one, which means an evaluation and exploitation of previously obtained results, with their adaptation to the specifics of european schools, and then a third reform taken on board, based on the responsibility and accountability of all social actors. on this last point, we believe that the european school should be seen as another model of schooling, a global one, in which the 'school after school' component has its effect. young people, from 2:30 to 5:00 during the semester or quarter, have a special schedule, but also during the summer holidays.

in particular, that what is needed, but this has already been said, is to ensure that we adopt the commission's proposals which are on the table and which concern all the elements of supervision, regulation and amendment of accounting standards. this is in the sense of adapting the regulation, of adapting the rules as is necessary in the present situation, and not of over-regulating. as has been said, we need more europe in this area and we need to adapt our regulation to the interdependence that binds financial institutions and our rules for financing the economy. we must quickly catch up with the backlog we have made in this area and regain the momentum we had a few years ago - you will be discussing this - in order to put into practice all the organization that had been put in place in the framework of mr lamfalussy's work. it is also important that the commission has its own powers, its own role to play in this area and the commission is quite right to insist on this. it is necessary to be perfectly logical in this respect. if we want to have more integration, if we want to provide the answers that we find effective in others, we need to set up an organization that is up to the financial challenges we will face, and we need to do it quickly. the french presidency, as i have said, will do everything in its power and will use all its energy to increase the necessary coordination and adaptation of the rules in this area. there must, of course, be - and there is - coordination between the european central bank, the ministers for economic affairs and finance and the commission in this area. it's more important than ever. we must find concrete answers to this and we must also anticipate the consequences that this crisis will have on the financing of the economy, on the economy. we're already seeing the first signs. and here too, and this is an essential element of confidence, innovative and important measures must be adopted in favour, in particular, of small and mediumsized enterprises. as regards the external relations aspects, which have been raised by president saryusz-wolski and mrs isler béguin, i would like to reply to president wolski that the european council will, as i have already said, have as its priority the definition of very precise guidelines and guidelines on energy security and solidarity. one crisis must not hide another. we had an energy crisis three months ago. it's still there. countries were dependent on other countries for energy supplies. it still stands. we must have a european energy policy that is real, and here too we have come too late and we must move quickly. as regards belarus, i wanted to tell president wolski that there will be a troika meeting on the sidelines of the general affairs council and that we will therefore be meeting the belarusian authorities. as you know, and as president wolski has stressed, we have expressed our concerns about the conduct of the elections. we are not satisfied with that. we will say so, but at the same time there is a discussion in the council about the possible relaxation of certain sanctions, in particular the visa bans against some of the belarusian officials who are the subject of the sanctions. we are still considering these developments in the council. i liked the formula you used, mr president, concerning the conflict between russia and georgia. we must indeed win peace and make sure that georgia wins it. this gives me an opportunity to reply to mrs isler béguin. we will hold a high-level conference on the evening of october 14 and october 15. the european union is also very happy that the situation in abkhazia and south ossetia - which i have to thank mrs isler béguin for, but which she knows very well - remains extremely isolated, because it is an unacceptable act that has been condemned very strongly by the european union and the presidency. as regards the pact on immigration, i would like to reply to mrs flautre - but i am sure that mrs isler béguin will share my observations with her - that what is changing in this pact is that there is better coordination, better harmonisation, particularly as regards asylum applications, as regards applications made by migrants. the pact clarifies the status of migrants, and this is a step forward for them. we are indeed in favour of a pragmatic vision, of a balanced approach, of an approach which can be read in the context of an enlargement of the schengen balances. the demographic crisis, the demographic challenge is also one of the challenges we must address under the french presidency. finally - and this is crucial, because it sums up everything - there is an interdependence between these crises too. these crises are linked. the economic and financial crisis is the most visible. but three months ago, it was an energy crisis. we are also facing a food crisis, a crisis of an external dimension. i repeat, to respond to these crises, to respond to these challenges, we need more europe, more coordination, more decision-making capacity, more readability and responsiveness. the answer to that is more institution. and the answer to that is that there are more institutions, and that is the lisbon treaty. we must ensure that this treaty enters into force as soon as possible. we must find a solution with our irish friends. we will work to ensure that by the end of the year we have a political solution to this institutional problem, which is urgently needed in view of the challenges we face and which we have discussed throughout the afternoon.

with mr purvis's statement on the need to take measures, within the responsibilities of each individual, to facilitate the recovery of the interbank market. it is essential. we cannot imagine that, aid, has sufficient clauses and provisions to deal with the respect for competition and the rules on state aid in a situation such as the present one with flexibility. and today, today or tomorrow, my colleague, commissioner kroes, will make public - as she announced yesterday at the ecofin council - guidelines on how the commission sees the flexibility margins of the treaty being used in this particular area, but avoiding discrimination between one solution and another, between one aid and another. he will also refer - and some of his colleagues have also mentioned this - to the implementation of the stability and growth pact. we reviewed it in 2005 and since then - i think i said it here the other day too - the consensus on the implementation of the revised pact has been total, one hundred percent, and yesterday, again, the ecofin council, as last saturday at the paris meeting, unanimously agreed that the current pact, as revised in 2005 - and this parliament also increase in public deficits - within the framework of the established rules, and not by setting aside the established rules. and that was clear in paris on saturday, it was clear yesterday at ecofin, it is clear here in today's debate, and i assure you that the commission will make sure that it is clear from now on, even though we are going to be living in very difficult circumstances, not only in the financial system but also in the real economy. tomorrow we're going to washington for the annual meetings of the international monetary fund. the international monetary fund's forecasts are again revised downwards. our forecasts for the next few weeks are going to be revised down. and this is not just an economic forecasting exercise, a theoretical exercise; unfortunately, this means less growth, less employment, more stressful situations on the labour market and, together with the inflationary pressure we are still suffering, although it has moderated in the last two months, it means in writing. – on 24 september i was asking in a written statement if europe is prepared to absorb the shock induced by its indissoluble link with the us market and if the eur 36.3 billion injected into the market by the ecb and bank of england is enough to make the danger disappear. a few days later fortis bank and dexia bank were also caught in the stream of the financial crises. furthermore, iceland’s banking system hit the ground (culminating with acquisition by the government of glitnir bank) and the uk government announced further money infusion (gbp 200 billion) in its economy. the events that have occurred so far provided an answer to my question that was posted as a rhetorical one. now, what is going to happen next? we know by now the financial institutions that were hit. the big ones. what we do not know is who else was hit and keeps the thrash hidden. what about the dozens of regional us banks who were involved in lending easy money in the housing sector? what about the european banks who could not stay far from investing in all kind of us exotic financial instruments that invaded the markets this decade?
in writing. the current global financial crisis, in addition to its transnational character, risks creating a state of major panic very quickly, not only in the financial-banking and economic world, but also among ordinary european citizens. i believe that, more than the seriousness of the economic phenomenon, which must be kept under financial and economic control, the danger of panic among the european citizens is of a far more serious nature and the effects of which will be remedied over a much longer period of time. that is why i am publicly calling on you, mr president, to do everything you can to resolve the current economic and financial crisis directly, immediately and effectively, and to act in public view so that the european public can feel protected by this european union, which was created precisely to provide a framework for protection in cases of extreme emergency. if we do not succeed in building european trust and solidarity now, there is a danger that everything that has been built up over 50 years will disappear in a single day.
rapporteur. − mr president, i am going to use this moment just to say a few words on issues which seem to frame the public debate on regulation and supervision. firstly, free markets are not synonymous with no regulations. a lax monetary policy can lead to higher inflation and eventually to recession but cannot by itself cause the meltdown of a financial system. the features of the financial system that have brought the threat of collapse are structural traits of the new financial system. the root cause of this crisis is an inadequately regulated financial system. mortgages are not toxic per se; badly constructed securities based on them are toxic. the packaging of financial products can bring a lot of opacity to markets. compensation schemes that make behaviour irresponsible: that is toxic. misleading models are toxic; extreme leveraging is bad. not to address these problems would be terribly wrong. not all financial innovation is benign. it is baffling therefore to hear that fresh regulation is bad because it would stifle financial innovation. building up proper regulation and supervision is not about bringing in socialism. it is about what kind of market economies we want to live in. that may lead to the recreation of elements of state capitalism, i agree, and that is for discussion. relying on industry-led initiatives is quite insufficient, for such initiatives frequently serve vested interests. why is it that we fail to learn from previous crises? clearly, vested interests can have a long arm and try to influence regulations and supervision, including the behaviour of people like us. do moral values matter? yes, i believe they do matter. the mess that we are in today is also because some believed that moral values do not matter in business. regulators and supervisors should understand that there are systemic risks. they should always be alert to financial stability. strains and crises cannot be entirely avoided, but we can limit the damage they cause. we need comprehensive answers to crises and genuine coordination among the eu, us and other major financial centres, particularly during bad times.
member of the commission. − madam president, can i briefly respond to a few points made. one relates to the previous debate, referred to by mr purvis. i was not invited to the previous debate. i would seldom pass up an opportunity of coming to the european parliament to hear regular fans of mine on the left praise my contribution to all things european. i could never miss an opportunity to hear people as eminent as mr schulz and mrs berès and many others speak about me in such glowing terms, so if i had been invited i would have gladly been here. regarding european solutions, i should like to give two examples. my predecessor initiated an item regarding pay; this was issued in the form of a recommendation, which is possibly the one of the softest instruments that the eu has at its disposal. that was the only chance it had of having anything accepted, because the competence in this regard lies with member states. we produced a report about a year and a half ago, but only one member state has implemented most of the recommendations. the others have, by and large, ignored it. the member state that implemented it – to give credit where credit is due – was holland. i am not saying it has implemented every exact letter of it, but it is the only member state that has gone down that particular road. so a european solution was there. a lot of comment is being made at the present time about the bonus culture and executive remuneration. we tried to come forward with a type of european solution, which was put forward by mr bolkestein – i think it was technically me who put it into effect but i give credit to mr bolkestein for initiating it. that is what we did, and that is what our report shows. secondly, regarding supervision – the main subject of this report – i have spoken on many occasions in the parliament and elsewhere about the issue of the cross-border supervision of financial institutions. i have spoken at ecofin and at press conferences. it is practically impossible to move forward on this particular issue because member states do not want us to have a european solution to this. however, i should like to point something out to members of the european parliament. last year i initiated the solvency ii proposal regarding insurance, and advanced the idea of colleges of supervisors, group supervision and group support. both in the council of ministers and in the negotiations with the european parliament, it has been watered down considerably. if we are to get this directive through in the lifetime of this particular legislature, a lot of heavy lifting will have to be done with the council of ministers because there are large divergences, not only on those particular items but on other items as well. although i have been in politics for all of my adult life, and have ceased to be amazed at contradictory positions that politicians may adopt – and no doubt, if you look over my long political career, you might find some of them as well – i still find it totally ironic and amazing that, when we advocate a european solution, for example regarding supervision to do with solvency ii, the people who advocate european responses – both ministers and members of the european parliament – are often the same people who come back and lobby for their own national state positions when a particular piece of legislation comes before them. those of us who were brought up in the catholic religion know the prayer of saint augustine which says more or less, ‘make me pure, but not just yet’. it is a bit similar here. this does not surprise me because i have been a politician for all of my adult life so i am used to that type of irony, to put it in its politest terms. be that as it may, there are only 44 or 45 cross-border financial institutions and we have a supervisory system which is way out of date for such operations. finally, may i make this point regarding the current crisis, which i have spoken about here and in other forums including press conferences. there is not one single magic bullet solution to all of this. if there had been, it would have been found long ago. these are unprecedented times and unprecedented responses have been given, both on this side of the atlantic and in the united states. can i just remind members here – and i am sure president barroso did so as well in his contribution – that we in the european commission do our best to coordinate and encourage member states to give a total response. but, as i said in my opening remarks, these responsibilities lie with member states, with member states’ central bankers and with member states’ ministries, because they are the elected people. they are the people who are in control of taxpayers’ monies and they are the people who must give the responses. we have attempted – and we have succeeded somewhat – to get a european response in some of these particular areas. may i finally make the point that we must remember the structure of europe. we are not a federation like the united states. we are not a central government, as found in the 27 member states, and therefore we can only act to the limit of the powers that are given to us.
rapporteur. − madam president, let me say something which, in my view, has not been properly outlined. regulation and supervision is not only about the building; it is about the object: what we regulate and supervise – and that is the crux of the matter. we could have had an independent, eu-wide oversight body regulating in europe and we would still have experienced the eruption of the crisis, because the problem is that the flaw lies in the financial system, not necessarily in the non-existence of a unique body of oversight and supervision. secondly, we are going to experience a very severe recession. we have to recapitalise the banks, and this will cost a huge amount of money. it is going to put tremendous pressure on public budgets, and i am asking myself – because we have to look at the broad picture – what is going to happen. i think that the current crisis shows that the size of the eu budget is nothing when the time comes to intervene and do something, so we have to rethink the eu budget. (the president cut off the speaker.)
in writing. the financial crisis that has engulfed almost the entire planet must be analysed at the level of the european union institutions. it is unacceptable that the world's youngest territorial organisation, the european union, cannot intervene in identifying a solution acceptable to all parties and insists on the creation of rapid action instruments, as defined by the ec's high-level study group. we are living in unprecedented historical times. we are on the verge of a financial collapse that threatens the eu's stated objectives, both for the 27 member states and for the rest of the world. every moment lost in administrative and bureaucratic procedures means huge losses to the international banking system, to the financial markets of all continents, and to the deterioration of the standard of living for all inhabitants. europe is obliged to take a stand and become a flagship in the fight to stop the current financial crisis. we now need to demonstrate the functionality of the system and the european institutions, we need coordination and collaboration between the governments of the member states, the european commission and the european parliament. we have the maturity and expertise to intervene in a situation that is dangerous for the future of the european union, but also for the future of humanity.
madam president, i want to warn against a policy which tends to reward the belarusian leadership in compensation for decisions of the russian leadership which we do not like. it is simply wishful thinking to believe that in this way we can generate a rift between moscow and minsk, or change the political orientation of president lukashenko. we should also not offer words for the liberation of prisoners who should not have been arrested. indeed, the european union must avoid the isolation of belarus and engage in dialogue with the leadership of the country. to this end, it must put in place a motivating package which should convince the regime, and the ordinary citizens who innocently support it, that the european union could contribute to improving the life of the belarusian people. on the other hand, any opening should be gradual, conditional, mutual and focused on principally bringing profit to society and not to the leadership. mr lukashenko stated that opposition is good in any country but not an opposition supported 100% from abroad. the problem is that the opposition in belarus could not survive because it is crushed by the regime. therefore we must not abandon the democratic opposition.
ladies and gentlemen, i want to take this opportunity to plead once again for greater involvement of the european union in improving health services in the member states of the european union. it is very true that the organisation of the health system is a matter for the member states, but the european community also has some powers, and the important role of the european community in the field of health has been reaffirmed in the lisbon reform treaty. the union's population is ageing, it is facing new threats: pandemics, physical and biological incidents, bioterrorism, to which we must all find solutions together. in addition, a mechanism for structured cooperation between member states, a mechanism for the exchange of information and good practice in the prevention, control and treatment of diseases in the countries of the european union should be developed. the directive on cross-border healthcare was a very good initiative. but i think it should be followed by other equally bold initiatives to improve the performance of the health system, because an important role we should be playing at european level is to achieve the goal of reducing health inequalities.
mr president, in romania we are unfortunately faced with a serious problem that endangers the safety and health of european citizens: the use in hospitals of sterile surgical thread imported from china. the romanian ministry of health had been aware of the problem since august, but despite warnings that it could cause illness or even death, it did not stop it in time. the alarm was raised after a patient died in hospital from an infection and other patients were in danger. i think this is a wake-up call not only for romania, but for the whole of europe. it is extremely serious that more and more products imported from china are raising questions and endangering the health and safety of european citizens. not long ago we had a problem with contaminated sweets from milk powder with melanin, also imported from china. we import products from china because they are cheaper, but i think europe should put the health of its citizens first. i ask commissioner vassiliou to launch an investigation to prevent any further incidents in the member states. we need urgent measures to verify these products to stop imports on the domestic market in time.
member of the commission. − madam president, could i first try to describe our huge disappointment after ten days of intensive negotiations in geneva. we felt that we were so close to being able to strike a deal on agriculture and nama, knowing very well that at the very end this would be the single undertaking that would determine whether the european union could consider a package to be acceptable. as the person responsible for agriculture, i must say it was extremely encouraging that for the first time ever european agriculture was not blamed for the failure of the discussions. the reason was that we have actually been doing our homework in the agricultural sector by reforming our common agricultural policy, first with the big reform in 2003 and then all the reforms after that period. so we were able to deliver an 80% reduction in trade-distorting domestic support, without actually damaging our agricultural sector. we had the possibility here to also lock the reforms into the multilateral trading system. it was not an agreement at any cost. it was a balanced agreement within those two areas. we could justify to the council that we were negotiating within the mandate given by the council to the negotiators. for agriculture, this mandate was simply not to force us into a new reform within the agricultural sector. i agree with those of you who have said that the multilateral system is important and necessary, because of the fact that it is only within the multilateral system that we can discipline, for example, trade-distorting domestic support and all other non-trade concerns. this can never be done in bilateral negotiations, so we have to stick to the values of the multilateral system. i also have to say that in these negotiations we never targeted the market of the developing countries. quite the opposite, actually, which was why the ssm was so important, as i said in my first intervention, in sheltering special products in the developing countries. i would like to add that we introduced the ‘everything-but-arms’ agreement back in 2002, which means that the european union today is by far the biggest importer of agricultural commodities worldwide. we are bigger than canada, the united states, australia and japan all together. so we have actually opened up our markets in the agricultural sector to these countries. food security has been mentioned here tonight as well. we have to realise that food security consists both of domestic internal production and of imports. if we look at the european union’s agricultural sector, we would never be able to be as strong as we are today if we had a closed market in agriculture. we have today, if i could take the country of the presidency, eur 7 billion in surplus trade in agricultural commodities. if we imagine that we closed our markets, we would never be able to sell all our high-quality products internally because we would be punished if we protected ourselves. others would do the same, which would prevent us from taking advantage of the emerging and increasingly open market opportunities for our high-quality products. so, of course we need a balanced approach. geographical indications (gis) were mentioned, but i did not raise this in my first intervention because of the time pressure and the chair’s very strong hand on time limits. gis are a crucial issue for the european union and we made it totally clear to the other negotiating partners that we would never be able to sign a deal if we did not have a positive outcome on geographical indications because this is so important, especially for high quality mediterranean products. i will reply briefly to mrs mcguinness. i do agree with you that we have actually been under-prioritising our development aid in the agricultural sector for decades. now that we see prices – not commodity prices, as it is right that prices have been going down today, but the prices of seeds and fertilisers – skyrocketing, we have suggested our facility to try and help the least developed countries, the poorest countries in the world, and put them in a position to buy seeds and fertilisers. this eur 1 billion facility is now being discussed here in parliament, and i hope that there will be a positive approach to this possibility of helping developing countries feed their own people and avoid migration from rural areas to the cities. please keep this in mind. it is very important.
in writing. – the failure of the doha trade round could be a harbinger of things to come, at a time when the deepening financial crisis puts tremendous strain on governments’ ability to play by the rules. benefits of free trade have been hailed against the backdrop of increasingly global markets. but free trade has to be fair and complemented by an international regime that helps poor countries develop. increasingly unequal incomes in wealthy economies and their fear of the rising power of some emerging economies are triggering bouts of protectionism. likewise, the struggle to control exhaustible resources and obtain basic commodities at affordable prices raises the propensity to restrict trade in many countries. one needs to mention here the increasingly complicated nature of geopolitics. the eu has to take the lead in mitigating the fallout from the current crises, in terms of preventing a collapse, de facto, of the multilateral trade and financial system. this lead includes, among other things, a reform of the ifis, involving the emerging global powers (brics) in dealing with global economic issues and a reform of the international architecture regulating the flow of finance. at end of the 19th century an international system that promoted free movement of goods and capital broke down and was followed by a devastating war in europe. we should remember this.
in writing. climate change can irreversibly affect all the planet's water resources and therefore adapting all compartments of socio-economic life to counteract the effects of water scarcity is essential. the european and international legislative frameworks offer effective leverage, but we need real progress in the accelerated practical implementation of all the measures envisaged, first of all those in the convention to combat desertification and those in the water framework directive, whose far too long implementation deadlines put the sustainability of resource security at risk. i call on the commission and the member states, through the active involvement of all relevant bodies and local authorities, to accelerate the process of transparent and coherent water use charging, based on the 'user pays' principle and eliminating losses from the networks. i also call for urgent implementation of concrete measures for the rational use of water bodies, especially those in which hydroelectric power stations are built and, in particular, the rivers that cool nuclear power stations, since the irrational use, combined with the sharp decline in flows, can lead to the closure of many clean electricity production facilities and, consequently, to the destabilisation of the european energy system, with major risks to the energy security of the union.
in writing. i wanted to speak because i am a member of parliament from the south of romania, an area that has been facing severe drought in recent years. the last one, in 2007, affected over 80% of households in my region, ialomiţa. i believe that this phenomenon can be reduced, that we can achieve results if we also treat it from the perspective of development, regional development. member states should be vigilant with regard to sensitive watersheds with water shortages, but especially with regard to the authorisation of economic activities in these sensitive areas. when allocating funds to water infrastructure, priority should be given to those that include clean technologies, that use water efficiently and that have considered risk prevention measures. i also believe that both the commission and the member states must promote a culture of water conservation in europe, based on management rules acquired through education. water scarcity is one of the new challenges. it has so far affected 11% of the european population and 17% of the union's territory. cohesion policy must meet this challenge. i would like to conclude by adding something else that we also urgently need to achieve results: the optimisation of the use of the solidarity fund and the civil protection cooperation mechanism.
in writing. water scarcity and drought have become major problems both within the european union and globally, especially in the context of climate change which has aggravated the situation. these have adverse side effects on biodiversity, water and soil quality and increase the risk of forest fires, as demonstrated by the devastating fires that have recently engulfed southern europe. in south-east europe, subsidies from the common agricultural policy have led to an increase in water consumption, which is why it is necessary to encourage total decoupling of aid and support for water management in rural development programmes. at the same time, the continuous increase in current demand for biofuels is forcing us to adapt production and other economic activities to the amount of water available locally. to find solutions to these problems, the transition to an economy based on efficient use and saving of water is a top priority. the introduction of water tariffs to stimulate rational use of water, the achievement of the objectives of the water framework directive and the correlation with other sectoral water policies must be reflected in actions to be undertaken in the future.
in writing. undeclared work is a phenomenon found in all eu member states and is a worrying feature of the european economic market, which is contrary to the principles of flexicurity. the fight against undeclared work is in some ways like the duel between microsoft and hackers. the more innovative our methods of combating undeclared work are, the more effective the fireworks employers use. and the best example is the emergence of 'grey work', where employers prefer to conclude employment contracts at the guaranteed minimum wage, the other side, up to the real wage, being paid 'black'. in romania, the phenomenon has taken on a particular scale, with grey work now accounting for 20 to 50% of total employment. worryingly, while early adopters of this method were found in microenterprises, today established names evade taxes and social security contributions and drive the employee toward a very small pension, which will put him on the brink of poverty. i have highlighted these aspects because the future strategy to combat undeclared work mentioned in the report must take into account the specificities of each member state. a unified european approach is needed, and effective collaboration between government agencies, labour inspectorates and the social partners.
in writing. nine years after the launch of the concept of 'decent work', half the world's workforce earns less than $2 a day, and the employment rate of women, relative to the whole population, was 49% in 2007, compared to the employment rate of men, which was 74.3%. in romania, only 15% of the total workforce has decent jobs, and the number of women at risk of poverty is about 10% higher than that of men. the pay gap is evident, with men earning more than women in most economic activities, with the monthly difference being about 1/3 of the country's minimum basic wage. the international labour organisation's study released on international women's day makes it clear that europe can no longer afford to ignore the potential of women and that access to the labour market and decent jobs is crucial to achieving gender equality. access to decent work for all citizens must be a priority of member states' employment policies, as it is the basic mechanism for social inclusion and the only sustainable solution to combating poverty.
in writing. road transport services account for 1.6% of gdp and provide jobs for 4.5 million eu citizens. the economy and society as a whole depend heavily on the efficiency of road transport, with 44% of goods being transported by truck and 85% of people using car, bus or coach. i consider that in order to comply with the legal provisions on social conditions, member states must invest in road transport infrastructure and must take the necessary measures to ensure the right level of investment for the development of road transport infrastructure. in this context, the construction of safe parking places should be a priority. in order to avoid artificial barriers to the free movement of goods, i have asked, by way of an amendment, for a report on the situation of traffic controls in each member state to be submitted to the european parliament by the commission. to the extent that there are types of controls that restrict the free movement of goods or persons, i have asked the commission to re-evaluate existing legislation and propose an amendment to it to ensure a uniform system of traffic controls.
the symbols of the european union assert its identity and can be decisive elements for communicating with the public and for its emotional attachment to the european institutions. parliament recognises and adopts the following symbols of the union: the flag, which is a circle of twelve gold stars on a blue background, the anthem, which is taken from the 'ode to joy' in ludwig van beethoven's ninth symphony and the motto 'united in diversity'. the flag is flown on all parliament grounds and at official events. by introducing the rules on the use of european union symbols in the european parliament into parliament's rules of procedure, parliament is sending a strong political signal. parliament celebrates europe day on 9 may, which is a day of national pride. i propose that the european parliament organise an annual europe day competition for young people to show how they see the future of europe and, above all, how they want to contribute to making this future a reality.
in writing. – the european union is without any doubt at a crossroads in its evolution, when it is of the utmost importance to acknowledge the need to move forward by tackling all the current complex issues that potentially could stalemate the dynamics of the european integration process. in this process, the european symbols are a crucial linking element for developing a positive identity at european level, complementary to and not replacing well-established national identities. the absence of the european symbols in the rejected lisbon treaty was most regrettable from the point of view of the critical democratic deficit currently confronting the european union. the claim that their inclusion in the lisbon treaty would be inappropriate turned out to be profoundly unrealistic for there is no doubt that they would not pose any peril to the concepts on which the eu was built. thus, in order to increase the popular support for and commitment to the european union in the forthcoming years, it is imperative to maintain and adjust these symbolic elements, so as to bind the european institutions and decision-making processes to acknowledgement of the ‘demos’ factor.
to respond to the major health challenges facing the european union, we need action plans that include health promotion, public education and disease prevention programmes, especially those related to diet, obesity, alcohol, drug and tobacco use. the detection, early diagnosis and appropriate treatment of chronic diseases, especially cancer, will ensure the quality of life of people affected by these diseases. the exchange of good practice within the european union in all areas of healthcare will therefore contribute to the improvement of citizens' well-being and health. it considers it important to promote healthy lifestyles in families, schools and the workplace in order to establish a healthy lifestyle and promote healthy ageing, both now and in the future. we must take special care of the interests of children by drawing up provisions on maternity and parental leave, taking into account the effects of the presence of parents on the physical and mental development of children. equally important is improving the health care system for pregnant women and informing them about the effects of tobacco and alcohol consumption.
in writing. it is gratifying that the european parliament has adopted the european commission's white paper together for health: a strategic approach for the eu 2008-2013. beyond the provisions on the health strategy, i note a drawback of the charter: the absence of quantifiable objectives to ensure its increased effectiveness. as the representative of a country with a poor quality healthcare system, reflected in a worrying state of health of the population, i would like to stress the importance of the charter's implementation in practice, but also the need for greater solidarity at the level of the european union to provide all its citizens with decent healthcare. romania holds many sad records in health. it is the eu's number one in tuberculosis and the penultimate in the quality of diabetes treatment, with diabetes being the most risky disease. one in ten romans suffer from liver disease. a quarter of the children have health problems. cancer mortality is rising alarmingly compared to the rest of the eu. the mortality rate from cardiovascular causes is 61% of all deaths, and in the eu 37%. romania is the european champion in prescriptions, hospitalisations and surgeries, but also the country with the lowest life expectancy in the eu.
in writing. i welcome the fact that the peterle report addresses and underlines the urgent need to take active measures to recruit and retain healthcare staff. according to the world health organization, the migration of two percent of a country's medical practitioners is code red for the authorities. in romania, 4% of romanian doctors applied for documents to go abroad to work, with the same proportion recorded throughout 2007. so not only have we passed this code red level, we've reached double the percentage. from the beginning of the year to september 1, 2008, 957 people applied for certificates of moral integrity from the college of doctors of romania (cmr) in order to work abroad. clearly, a health system cannot function without doctors. i believe that this phenomenon is of concern not only for romania but for the whole of europe, and the issue of the lack of qualified people to treat european patients should be of the utmost concern to the member states, but also to the union.
in writing. health is one of the most important values in people's lives. the alarming increase in cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and obesity, despite advances in the treatment of these diseases, is a major problem we face. the problems of overweight, as well as undernutrition, poor diet and hiv/aids, are health-threatening challenges in the european union. the differences in cancer survival are so great between the new and the old eu countries that we can speak of an 'iron curtain on health'. the european union must strengthen its actions to reduce inequalities between member states, in particular by exchanging good practice in different areas, as well as by promoting public education for better health care, by supporting innovation in health systems, and by proposing implementation mechanisms for structured cooperation between eu institutions. we need to define core health values, an eu health indicator system and ways to reduce health inequalities. we need to invest in health, we need to take measures to promote health at all ages, we need to take measures on tobacco, food, alcohol and other factors that affect health.
co-rapporteur. − mr president, also as an acknowledgement of the frantic search by eu member states to rescue the banking system, but not in a sufficiently coordinated way, we have thought that it makes sense to introduce this amendment. it reads: ‘whereas the increasing cross-border nature of banking in europe and the need to respond in a coordinated way to adverse shocks, as well as the need to deal with systemic risks effectively, require divergences between the national regimes of member states to be reduced to the greatest extent possible; whereas there is a need to move beyond the studies that the european commission has already carried out in this regard and to amend directive 94/19/ec as soon as possible to provide the same level of protection for bank deposits across the whole european union in order to preserve financial stability and depositors’ confidence and avoid distortions of competition’.
in writing. − on 8 february 2009, a referendum will be held in switzerland on the extension of the free movement agreement with the european union and its extension to romania and bulgaria. according to swiss parties, the referendum is meant to stop the 'uncontrolled mass immigration' from romania and bulgaria. switzerland held a similar referendum in september 2005, following the 2004 enlargement wave. fortunately, the result of this referendum was positive. we should not dispute the right of any state to hold a referendum, but i think that each of the member states must be sure that the european union will be in solidarity, whatever the outcome of that consultation.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the recommendation of mr marian jean marinescu (a 6-0343/2008) on the following grounds: 'every citizen of the european union has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states'. article 45 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union provides for this, and the treaty of rome stated as early as 1957 that 'any discrimination on grounds of nationality is prohibited'. as new member states of the european union, it is only natural that both bulgaria and romania should participate in the signature of the protocol to the ec/switzerland agreement on the free movement of persons, benefit from its provisions and enjoy the same rights as all european states. otherwise, there could be no true 'european citizenship' in accordance with the maastricht treaty (1993).

in writing. - i voted for the report on speeding up the fight against undeclared work, because the phenomenon of undeclared work is a pressing problem throughout the community. the spread of black labor is largely the result of excessive taxation and bureaucracy, leading to a significant decrease in tax revenues and, by implication, under-filling of the budget. moreover, informal hiring also encourages unfair competition. in this context, in addition to the increased attention that the authorities should pay to reducing taxes on the labour market and cutting red tape, i stress the need to stimulate new job creation and to regulate temporary and casual employment flexibly.

mr president, the real test for any institutional structure, including the eu, is in time of crisis, and we are in a time of crisis. the integration of the so-called new members is not complete, the treaty of lisbon is not yet ratified by all member states and our dependence on imported energy is increasing. unfortunately, although indispensable, common action often comes slowly and with difficulty, because members prefer the individual approach. if we let the latter prevail over the former, our union is in great danger – irrespective of the moral aspect that those who have benefited most from it have more obligation to see that it gets stronger and not weaker. and the same goes for nato too. now, more than ever, we need common analyses, common perceptions, common positions and common action with regard to the increasing challenges we are confronted with. let us do this so we will not be accused of wasting the most remarkable example of successful cooperation on a continent ravaged by wars for too long.
last week's european commission legislative proposal on illegal logging should have been a great victory for all those who have campaigned against illegal logging over time. but the commission has chosen to tackle a real problem with a minimalist and even fanciful solution. there is no standard on the legality of timber, suppliers do not have to prove the legality of products, and possession and trade of timber are not recognised as criminal offences. if everyone can create standards as they please and there is no independent public monitoring mechanism, then the european union is only encouraging current illegal practices. it is a shame to congratulate each other and to say that we have done a good job when, in fact, the control of the legality of wood on the eu market remains very lax. the european parliament must take a more ambitious stance in the fight to stop uncontrolled deforestation. i therefore call on my colleagues from all the political groups to work together to significantly improve the commission's proposal. only through a clear and effective law will we send a strong message to suppliers that we do not tolerate the trade in illegal timber in the eu.
