the rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on transport and tourism. − the directive introduces green criteria among the criteria analysed for the purchase of clean and energy-efficient public road transport vehicles. member states shall inform the authorities and contracting parties providing public passenger transport services of the provisions relating to the purchase of environmentally friendly vehicles. the tran committee proposes that member states and the commission consider the eligibility for financial assistance of projects dedicated to urban mobility and the promotion of green vehicles in the mid-term review of the national strategic reference frameworks and national and regional operational programmes. urban transport initiatives such as the civitas and smart energy europe programmes must also be continued. the tran committee proposed the use of the inscription 'energy-efficient and clean urban road transport' by authorities whose purchases of green vehicles are included in the total of specific annual purchases. i congratulate the rapporteur and i am convinced that this document will change the behaviour of local public authorities towards the environment.
the directive makes local authorities aware of the environmental impact of urban transport. member states may apply stricter award criteria for the purchase of clean and energy-efficient vehicles than those proposed in the directive and may opt for the purchase of retrofitted vehicles or upgrade existing vehicles by adding particulate filters or adapting engines to less polluting fuels. i personally believe that the purchase of clean and energy-efficient road transport vehicles, including the subsequent installation of engines and spare parts in these vehicles, when they have not exceeded 75% of their total mileage over their lifetime, should be possible. this directive shall not apply to the retrofitting of engines and spare parts to road transport vehicles when they have exceeded 75% of their total lifetime mileage. i think these elements are necessary because this is an investment that has to be sustainable.
in writing. the introduction of clean and energy-efficient vehicles on the market will make a significant contribution to environmental protection, improving air quality and making transport more energy-efficient by reducing pollutant emissions. the objectives of the air quality directive and those of the green paper on sustainable urban mobility can be more effectively implemented by promoting green public transport. at the same time, japan's car industry, which is very focused on making clean cars, is a threat to the european union market, which needs to invest more in the technological development of low-carbon vehicles and in the promotion of alternative fuels. in order to encourage car manufacturers to produce as many green cars as possible, it is necessary that public procurement takes into account the lifetime costs of those vehicles and their impact on the environment and public health. these requirements will not, however, distort competition between the public and private sectors, as long as the latter are subject to the same environmental rules and criteria in the provision of public transport services.
mr president, let me put this straight. i am committed to fighting terrorism and to ensuring security for all citizens, but i am not going to explain to my constituents how 11 meps decided, in an obscure bureaucratic procedure, to allow body-scanning in european airports which would show them naked. this whole comitology procedure is yet another example of how to push european citizens into euro-scepticism. the commission’s argument – but also that of the developers of this technology – is that body scanners are intended as alternative to physical searches. but the moment we allow this technology, we will have no guarantee that it will not be used for primary screening. we all know from our experience in airports that some of them perform a mandatory physical search. therefore the issue is whether we allow body scanners or not. perhaps we should forbid them. so i urge the commission to suspend this procedure, which has put us in a messy situation. we need to have a large democratic debate in which parliament and the edps have to be involved. this is invasive technology, and issues such as privacy, proportionality and efficiency must be carefully looked into.
i'm going to assume that the safety of passengers in the aviation sector is paramount. but body scanning involves taking detailed images of the human body. these images invade people's private space. i'd like to refer to the conditions under which these images are used. commissioner, we understand that the footage will not be stored. but are they used in compliance with all the requirements of the legislation on the protection of personal data? what measures are you planning to take to ensure that staff using these scanners are aware of and comply with the provisions of personal data legislation? commissioner, even if the passengers agree to use these scanners, i'd like to be sure that the images are erased. the health effects of using these scanners, unfortunately, will only be deduced after a number of years.
the creation of harmonised criteria for the approval and administrative management of any changes to marketing authorisations for medicinal products will benefit patients who will have access to better and safer products in the long term. given that only 20% of medicines for human and veterinary use are authorised through community procedures, this revision of the directive will have a considerable impact on the pharmaceutical market in the european union. any changes in the production process, packaging or manufacturer's address should be reviewed and simplified to ensure better protection of public health. we need to create a simple and flexible legislative framework so that all medicinal products, regardless of the procedure applied in the marketing authorisation process, are subject to the same evaluation and approval criteria. this will ensure the free movement of medicines within the european union by dispensing with the controls necessary to guarantee the quality of imported medicines and will determine the establishment and effective functioning of the internal market. both consumers and the pharmaceutical industry will have rapid access to the latest generation of medicines, as long as differences in national provisions are removed and a harmonised system is created.
i firmly believe that the draft directive represents important progress in ensuring faster access to medicines and i congratulate the commission, commissioner verhaugen and the rapporteur on this initiative. because the free movement of goods is one of the basic principles of the internal market and it seems to me that this principle should apply to medicinal products. the complexity and diversity of administrative procedures for authorising modifications to medicinal products already on the market distorts the functioning of the internal market itself. of course, besides the pharmaceutical industry and the authorities having to deal with bureaucracy, the primary victims are the patients, who because of these complex procedures benefit from delayed improvements in medicines. i therefore fully support the commission's proposal to harmonise the procedures for authorising modifications to medicinal products, irrespective of the initial authorisation procedure, as this simplification will make the whole system more efficient and, above all, guarantee a high level of protection of public health. i also support the rapporteur, mrs grossetête, on the need for a single procedure for authorising changes which affect authorisation more. a final comment on the commission's proposal to retain the original name of the medicinal product in the event of an extension of authorisation: i support retaining the original name, as even frequent change of the name of medicinal products may confuse patients who must consult a doctor before treatment anyway and who is normally aware of the new therapeutic indications of the medicinal product.
in many european countries, the procedure for authorizing medicines is still well regulated formally, but i would draw attention to the fact that too rapid authorization procedures lead to many deaths, caused by overdoses of medicines or by drugs taken by accident or by medicines with side effects that have not been sufficiently explored before. i think it's too easy to put new, improved drugs on the market, with miraculous properties, but they're taken off the market in a very short time. who is responsible for their quality and the side effects they produce? we welcome the initiative to introduce a harmonization procedure unanimously accepted in europe, but new medicines should be subject to an analysis by an international panel of experts.
in writing. the european union needs clear and strict rules on the conditions for placing medicines on the market, and also on all medical products in general. i would like to illustrate this need with a recent case in romania. in september, a woman died after an operation using surgical thread imported from china that had not been sterilized. other patients have suffered life-threatening complications. the commission of inquiry of the romanian ministry of health unequivocally acknowledged that the surgical dog in question did not bear the ce quality markings. the law on conformity assessment of products clearly demonstrates that the main blame lies with the relevant ministry, but clearer rules and more transparency could have prevented this.
in writing. although medicinal products in the european community continue to be subject to regulation by national and community governments throughout their existence, discrepancies between commission regulations and member states' provisions have negative consequences for public health, administration and the overall functioning of the internal pharmaceutical market. the aim of this report is to ensure that all medicinal products placed on the community market, including those authorised at national level, are subject to the same approval criteria and administrative changes, irrespective of the procedure by which these medicinal products have been authorised. the proposal simplifies administrative procedures for member states and allows for the harmonisation of assessment and surveillance requirements for all medicinal products. the adoption of this report will provide much greater protection for consumers who will directly benefit from the efficiency improvements, strengthened organisation and clarity and transparency that are the response to the implementation of a simplified and standardised regulatory system for marketing authorisations for medicinal products in the european union.
our goal is always to ensure legislation that brings more benefits to the consumer. that is why i would like to endorse this new directive which brings a model and simplified framework for timeshare holiday products. i welcome the proposals to give consumers a 14-day cooling-off period to withdraw from a contract and to prohibit the demand for advance payments within that period. i hope that the amendments will contribute to a functioning internal market by harmonising european legislation in this field and thus increasing the level of consumer protection. we must ensure that, when the contract is signed, the consumer is fully informed and that all the necessary pre-contractual information is made available to him about the costs involved, the services he will benefit from. we need to encourage the development of the holiday products industry in time-share and long-term; to increase consumer confidence in buying holiday packages across borders and always encourage businesses to sell across borders, to take advantage of the benefits of the single market. i ask commissioner kuneva to intervene in credit agreements too, because after this financial scandal in which we find ourselves most banks have changed these credit agreements too, continuing to deceive consumers. i congratulate the rapporteur on her work and hope that we will have a market that benefits the consumer.
in writing. −the report on the need for a european parliament and council decision on a community programme to protect children from the avalanche of pornography and violence flooding the internet and other communication technologies is more than welcome, although it was too much to expect. was it necessary to wait to see children killing children or children raping children to make such a decision? such realities were hard to imagine a few years ago in european society. and all this because globalisation, which means cross-border communication, has made information, instead of being a package of truth, of education, of beauty, a commodity whose sole purpose is to make a profit at any cost, and to get a rating. that is why the report must be taken very seriously by the council and the commission, if we do not want our own children to lead the future society towards crime, violence and pornography. i voted for this report in the hope that it could trigger the process of drawing up a directive to block children's access to inappropriate content, while respecting citizens' right to information.
in writing. −this directive introduces a harmonised methodology for the procurement of 'clean' and energy-efficient vehicles for the provision of sustainable public transport services; it also contributes to the priorities set in the context of the lisbon strategy. an explicit requirement that all purchases of road transport vehicles by public authorities and by operators providing services under a contract with a public authority, as well as purchases of road transport vehicles for the provision of public passenger transport services, take into account energy consumption, carbon dioxide emissions and pollutant emissions. the greatest economic gain would be achieved by making external costs mandatory as an award criterion in all procurement decisions. vehicle owners would directly benefit from the long-term energy savings, which would far exceed a possibly higher vehicle price. promoting 'clean' and energy-efficient vehicles through public procurement for the provision of public transport services stimulated by this initiative will accelerate the development of these technologies on the market and contribute to energy saving, environmental protection and public health.
in writing. −i voted for the jørgensen report on the promotion of environmentally friendly vehicles for public transport. the original proposal submitted by the commission in 2005 was rejected by parliament as too bureaucratic and not reducing pollution. the old proposal called for 25% of cars to be green. the new proposal concerns only motor vehicles intended for public transport and the public authorities responsible for providing these services. i believe that the new proposal will enable local decision-makers to become more aware and to take more firm action to protect the environment. at european level, the costs of congestion in large urban areas are estimated at 1% of european gdp. pollution in large cities can be reduced by promoting public transport and, above all, by clean public transport. in addition to the promotion of metros, trams, trolleybuses, regional trains or shipping, pollution can also be reduced in large european cities by introducing eco-buses. the new directive introduces an obligation for local authorities to calculate and take account of the cost of using a bus or minibus for its entire operating life. i congratulate the local authorities in prague on the acquisition, on the basis of state aid, of a fleet of environmentally friendly buses, thus setting an example to be followed.

in writing. when you say bosnia, you are talking about another page in the long-suffering history of the balkan peninsula. the bosnian war destroyed over 75 percent of the country, resulting in over 200,000 deaths and 1.8 million refugees. the signing of the eu's association and stabilisation agreement came 13 years after the end of the war. vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be able to speak in this debate which is intended to commemorate the great famine of 1932 and 1933, which was one of the great tragedies of the 20th century. after many years of silence, the testimony of that suffering is now coming to our attention alongside the stories of the many survivors who were involved in that terrible event. it is vital that we do not forget what happened in the holodomor. the story of the great famine not only illustrates the tragedy of the ukrainian people but reminds us once again of what human beings are capable of. but the holodomor also teaches us something important: the sacrifice of so many dead was not in vain. that sacrifice reminds us that no state should ever accept the subjugation of individuals, whatever the cause or purpose for this. this disastrous famine has shown the superiority of a constitutional state over one in which no form of dissent is allowed. tragedies like the holodomor only happen in those human societies that trample on citizens' rights, the rule of law and democratic principles. the european union was built on the ashes of war and various totalitarian experiences, on the ashes of dictatorships which have deeply wounded the history of europe and the world. but from those same tragedies and catastrophes came the democracies of europe, and in the last fifty years, a season of peace has been built on those ruins which we have a duty to defend, to carry beyond the borders of the union: the european union has been a major force in the world for over 50 years, and it has been the most important achievement of a united europe. today ukraine has changed as well. in this independent country, a member of the council of europe and a signatory to the european convention on human rights, as well as to numerous other international instruments for the safeguarding of these fundamental rights, ukraine has a tremendous opportunity to prove itself, to strengthen itself as a democratic state that respects human rights and the rule of law. this is certainly an ambitious and difficult task. we have seen how many political battles and struggles have marked the last few years of the history of this country, which has become stronger in its democracy. it is necessary at this historic moment that we all support, encourage, with our political support, the independence of the judiciary. it is important to continue to fight corruption and to take account of the outcome of the recent electoral consultations in order to ensure that democratic principles are respected. nor should the protection of the weakest and the most marginalized, whatever their race, ethnicity or religion, or their sexual orientation or state of health, be neglected in that country. the european union will continue to support ukraine in these important efforts. at the same time, we will continue to work alongside our ukrainian partners to increase prosperity for all citizens of that country, opening up new markets and increasing prospects for economic activity and investment, as well as intensifying contacts between our citizens. i would like to add, as commissioner for transport, that also with regard to the transeuropean networks, we must remember that they can not only serve to strengthen our internal market but are also a tool to widen europe's borders, to open europe to new horizons, to strengthen the link between countries bordering on the european union, between neighbours and friends, such as ukraine. there can be no better tribute to the victims of the holodomor than the creation of a prosperous, stable and democratic ukraine, based on strong institutions and a committed civil society. only if this goal is achieved will the sacrifice of so many innocent victims not have been in vain.
on behalf of the pse group.– madam president, this is a very special debate. as a political body, the european parliament is asked to legislate and to provide executive decision-makers with political guidance for properly coping with the challenges, opportunities and dangers of our present times. in other words, we are history-builders and not historians. we are not asked to judge the past, but to build the present, and are supposed to be judged by the future. therefore, the socialist group reluctantly accepted to subscribe to a resolution which apparently aims to establish a historical truth about a tragic event that took place in ukraine in the past. we did that, however, because we understood that solidarity with the ukrainian people and their sufferings could mobilise ukrainians in their efforts to unite their country, to democratise it, modernise it and bring it inside its natural family which is the european union. at the same time, we understood that if the tragedies and crimes of the past are forgotten, the danger of their being repeated is overwhelming. historical condemnation of crimes cannotprovide reparation for the victims thereof or their heirs, but it is moral compensation. moreover, it is an intellectual and political guarantee against repetition of the crimes and resurrection of the bad instincts that lay at their origin. by condemning old totalitarian crimes, we not only shame the criminals of the past, but also those who might think to apply the same criminal methods in the future. awareness that impunity is impossible might very well stop them doing so. we must proclaim today that there is no state rationale, no social objective and no ideological principle that can excuse a crime such as the holodomor, the artificial famine which caused so much suffering for so many innocent people in a crazy attempt to destroy the moral dignity, national pride and biological existence of the great ukrainian people. at the same time, while condemning the crimes, expressing solidarity with the victims, and denouncing this attempt to destroy a whole people, we cannot put the blame for those crimes on another people. the holodomor was the product of a totalitarian political regime. all the peoples that were subject to that regime were victims of various similar crimes and hardships. the discussion today should not only remind us that we must always stay united against totalitarianism, but also that the present ukrainian generation, on behalf and in the memory of the holodomor victims, must eliminate from their country and their history all authoritarian instincts, inclinations and practices. they have to consolidate their national unity and accomplish together their democratic ideals. likewise, our expression of solidarity should inspire the ukrainians to solidarity and reconciliation, both inside and outside their country. inside, with their countrymen, who belong to different ethno-cultural groups, and outside with our neighbours. that is one of the best ways in which they could become members of the european union, and, if they choose to take that way, it means that our debate this evening has not been futile. eu membership for ukraine would be the best historical reparation that the ukrainians themselves can offer to the victims of holodomor.
i would like to congratulate mr stockmann on his work in obtaining a common position of the council with a view to adopting the directive laying down common principles for the charging of airport charges at community airports. for airport users, the proposed legislation provides a framework for the setting of charges that involves decision-making, is transparent and allows for appeal. the council accepted parliament's proposal to limit the scope to airports with an annual traffic of more than 5 million passengers and to the largest airport in each member state. the differentiation of airport charges must be based on transparent, objective and clear criteria. the common position requires airports to operate on the basis of cost-effectiveness criteria and will allow incentives for new routes to disadvantaged and peripheral regions. however, they must be granted on the basis of transparent criteria. we support the idea that, after informing the commission in accordance with community legislation, member states may authorise an airport managing body to apply a common and transparent charging system to airports serving the same city or conurbation, provided that each airport fully complies with the transparency requirements laid down in the directive. the environmental criteria will also become a basis for the adaptation of airport charges. the airport managing body shall publish decisions on changes to the charging scheme at the latest two months before they enter into force. as regards pre-financing of airport investments, member states should refer to icao policies or establish their own security measures. parliament considered that the independent supervisory authorities should be able to delegate the implementation of the provisions of the directive to other independent supervisory authorities under their full responsibility, provided that the same standards are met.

mr president, commissioner, the 15% difference between the wages of women and men for the same work is real. in the case of female managers, this rises to 20%, and in the case of sme managers, it even reaches 30%. 28% of women researchers in industry and only 34% of women in industry have more than one child. commissioner, during the period of maternity leave, the average annual percentage for calculating the pension for these periods translates into a financial loss, despite the social importance of this period. mothers should not be penalized for giving birth and caring for a child in the first few months of life. i also think that child support should not be given only to mothers who worked in the 12 months before the birth. i believe that it is not the child's fault whether or not his mother worked during this period and, above all, i believe that there should be no discrimination between children from the moment they are born.
the principle of equal opportunities and equal treatment between women and men is a subject with specific connotations in the newly integrated countries of eastern europe. the benchmarks of professional performance are retained in their deeply masculinized essence and this perspective cannot be easily changed in the ex-communist space where, following the propaganda effort of the regime, the collective mind has taken over a model of completely artificial equality. the lack of consistency of primitive egalitarianism promoted by the propaganda of communist regimes has led to a undermining of modern efforts to promote equal treatment between women and men. based on these premises, i appreciate that any modern effort to promote the principle of gender equality must focus on a broader educational dimension, to provide eu citizens with realistic systematic models of non-discriminatory treatment. the implementation of this principle in the community requires that the european institutions propose more than just the organisation of a european day for equal pay.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, their use must take account, in addition to abstract theories, of the concrete situations in the member states. at the same time, we must maintain consistency with the broader principles of the policies we pursue. for example, the principle of equal treatment. the present report would fulfil both conditions if a proposal were accepted, in particular amendment no 69, which refers to the maintenance of duty-free at union customs offices other than ports and airports until 2017. this amendment removes a discrimination between those who travel by water or air and those who travel by land, which is absolutely unjustified from an economic, theoretical and practical point of view. at the same time, it confers a certain advantage on those living in the border areas, as already mentioned. they are generally economically disadvantaged because of their peripheral status and the loss of jobs would affect them negatively. ladies and gentlemen, there are good reasons to accept this amendment on the vote tomorrow; given the huge expense we're willing to make to rescue the corporations, this exemption has minor financial implications.
mr president, commissioner, chapter 4 sets out the basic provisions and procedures applicable to the computerised system for monitoring the movement of excisable products. the new feature is the introduction of the system and the administrative document in electronic format. in order to ensure the efficient operation of the computerised system, member states should adopt, within the national applications, a uniform data set and data structure to provide economic operators with a reliable interface. the transitional period for adapting to the computerised system for monitoring the movement of excise goods under suspension of excise duty should take into account the feasibility of putting the computerised system into operation in each member state. to this end, member states and the commission shall take the necessary measures to implement the public key infrastructure at national level and to ensure its interoperability. commissioner, in view of the food crisis that is coming and the social and economic importance of european agriculture, i believe that we should consider the possibility of eliminating excise duties on fuel used for agricultural work and on energy used to pump water for irrigation.

in writing. firstly, i welcome both the commission's initiative and the rapporteur's position, as i believe that substantial progress has been made on the migration of highly skilled labour, which is essential for achieving the lisbon objectives. i believe, however, that the eu must be attractive not only to skilled workers from third countries but also to young europeans. given that the eu's economic competitiveness is at stake, we do not want to see a 'brain drain' in favour of the us or canada and against the eu. the current initiative must therefore also be strengthened by a policy to stimulate european young people. we also need to act with great caution and responsibility, taking into account the situation of human resources in certain areas in the countries of origin of these migrants, in order not to contribute to the deepening of the human resources crisis, especially in education and health. finally, i support mrs klamt's position on the application of community preference in recruitment and the idea of giving priority to the citizens of the new member states who are still subject to restrictions on access to the labour market. in the event of these restrictions being maintained, this priority seems to me to be a minimum condition for the citizens of these countries not to feel like second-class european citizens.
in writing. i would like to draw attention to some provisions that may have a discriminatory effect and therefore ask you to consider giving priority to citizens of the new eu member states in accessing the eu labour market over immigrants from outside the eu. the 'blue card' initiative is welcome, as it will partially address the shortage of highly skilled labour and can play an important role in reducing illegal immigration. however, there are provisions that disadvantage citizens from countries that have recently joined the european union. as access to the labour market for romanians in most eu countries is still restricted, either in full or in certain areas, i believe it is necessary to oblige the member states to reject blue card applications in those sectors where access for workers from the newly acceded countries is still restricted by the current transitional provisions. residents of eu countries, both new and acceding ones, must have priority over those outside the union. i also want to warn about the risk that the 'brain drain' in the developing world will affect areas that are essential to them, such as health, education and research, leading to a boomerang effect with complex implications on a global scale.
in writing. the creation of the blue book, which the eu needs as it faces a shortage of skilled workers in certain sectors, is a step forward for the economic migration of highly skilled workers from third countries. however, the blue paper may be a step backwards if member states do not reject requests for its release for labour market sectors to which access for workers from the new member states is restricted by the transitional measures provided for in the accession treaties. i cannot help recalling that england and ireland have already expressed their wish to maintain the labour market restrictions for romania and bulgaria for another three years. i would point out that the application of the policy of the blue book directive would put european citizens at a disadvantage compared with those in third countries. although the principle of community preference is mentioned in this directive, it is clear that it will not be possible to apply it to those european citizens who have restrictions on certain sectors of the european labour market. i would ask you to vote in favour of the amendment concerning this clarification, so that we do not end up in a situation where economic migration from third countries takes precedence over free movement between countries within the union. the new member states' logical desire is not to feel like second-class eu members.
in writing. demographic deficits and an ageing population in the european union put us at risk of the labour market, health and pension systems being put at risk. under these conditions, the blue card comes as a counterweight to the american green card system, which has proved to be a real success, considering that about 50% of the highly skilled workforce choose the us or canadian market. i think it is essential to have a uniform immigration system for all 27 member states, so that every eu country can benefit from the added value of a highly skilled workforce. it is equally important to me that the eu gives due recognition to these professionals by offering them fair and non-discriminatory pay. i would not like to end without mentioning that the eu labour market is not yet fully open to workers from the new member states, so we must be very careful that the measures we adopt do not discriminate against de facto citizens of the european union.
president of the council. - mr president, mr vice-president of the european commission, mr verheugen, ladies and gentlemen, mr pribetich, your speech and your questions are particularly relevant and, given the momentum you have given to supporting them and asking them, it will be particularly difficult for me to speak after you. the european union has a long history of cooperation with the united states and other countries in the space sector. its missions contribute to the increase of our knowledge, both in terms of earth observation and oceanography and in satellite meteorology. it also corresponds to the growth of our economies through telecommunications and satellite navigation. it has become, quite quietly, but essentially, a tool that is part and parcel of modern life. space is also a tool, as you have said, which makes it possible to unite europe around a common ambition and develop european identity. and it is in this spirit that the french presidency, together with valérie pécresse, organized the first informal meeting of european space ministers in kourou, europe's space port, last july. i know that mr rovsing represented the european parliament at this event, and i thank him for that. the meeting provided a common vision for europe in space around the three main actors of european space policy: the union, the european space agency and the member states, while recognising the union's increased responsibilities. these three players will make europe one of the leading space powers on the international stage, rest assured. in order to develop a european space policy that benefits all europeans, it is first necessary to guarantee free and fair access for all member states of the union to the benefits of space activities; secondly, to strengthen existing coordination mechanisms in the field of space, european expertise and community-funded investments, through intergovernmental and national sources; finally, we must also improve the synergies between civil and defence space programmes. so this is how the union, the european space agency and the member states will ensure that we have access to space that is autonomous, reliable and at the best cost, which is necessary in relation to our major partners. of course, this requires a stronger role for the european union in the european space policy. it is the union's responsibility to federate demand for space applications, to identify user requirements, to set priorities and to ensure continuity of services. we have also developed community financial instruments and schemes at union level to take account of the specificities of the space sector in the context, in particular, of the forthcoming financial perspective. the space council held on 26 september last allowed the two flagship programmes, galileo egnos and the gmes programme, to be put into orbit, if i may say so, and to be confirmed. regarding galileo egnos, the european union has signed a number of cooperation agreements with third countries, such as the united states, china, israel, south korea, ukraine and morocco. the same council of 26 september stressed the importance of increased coordination between the commission, esa and the member states in the field of research and development, particularly for satellite navigation systems. as regards the gmes programme, the forthcoming council meetings on 1 and 2 december are expected to lay down the guidelines and define the terms of the partnership between the union and the member states, make legislative proposals formalising the programme before the end of 2009, and i can already tell you that the council considers that the public good approach is the one to be adopted for the proper development of this programme. a data policy must also be put in place quickly. finally, there must be four priorities, which were also mentioned by mr pribetich: the first is space and climate change, since the contribution of space applications is unique in this field; the second is the contribution of space activities to the lisbon strategy; the third is everything that has to do with space and security so that we can have, at european level, monitoring and surveillance of european space infrastructure and space debris. the fourth priority is space exploration, which is a political and global undertaking and europe should act within a global programme. to this end, europe must develop a common vision and long-term strategic planning and also have the necessary political dialogue with other states in the context of wider international cooperation and, in this regard, the council welcomes the commission's announcement that it will organise in 2009 a high-level political conference on the long-term global vision for space exploration. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the european council has been a very important meeting. i am very grateful to mr pribetich for giving me the opportunity to begin a contribution on a very technical subject with a line from a poem by my favourite french lyricist, guillaume apollinaire: 'il est grand temps de rallumer les étoiles'. i believe that the french presidency has already done a great deal to give european space policy the place in our work that it really deserves. we have made great progress in recent years, we have a european space policy for the first time - we have never had that before. we have a framework for a common european policy in which the commission plays a coordinating role. we have reached a broad consensus on the strategic, ecological and economic importance of space policy for europe. no one disputes this, and i would like to highlight here the meeting of the space council at the end of july at the kourou spaceport in french guiana, where we saw for the first time that europe is ready for this new venture into space. we have also shown that the european space industry is extremely efficient. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. europe is a leader in satellite technology, europe is a leader in vehicle technology. we have the best carrier systems in the world. we have an infrastructure with kourou that doesn't exist anywhere else in the world. we have demonstrated the state of european space technology by our contribution to the international space station, the space laboratory. i'm also very pleased that esa has done a whole series of successful exploration missions in our solar system that others have failed to do. so we have no reason to hide behind other europeans. we have achieved excellent cooperation between the european commission and esa, and the division of labour is working perfectly smoothly. in view of this smooth cooperation, there is not the slightest reason to think about changing structures in this area. but there are still problems to be solved. we europeans have no independent access to space. we can't transport people up and down. we have to decide whether we want to be dependent on others here for the long term or not. i don't want to hide my personal opinion from you. europe needs independent and secure access to space. we will also have to deal with the question of what the next major missions in the exploration of our solar system are. my view is that these next great missions can only be seen as the task of all of humanity. we should avoid any national or regional competition. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. this will be the subject of the conference which minister jouyet has just spoken of and which the commission will be organising next year. so just to make this clear to everybody, we really want to talk about what the next big challenge is beyond the purely technical application of space-based technologies. what's the next big task, the next big goal, to satisfy the human urge to explore space? space-based technology is absolutely essential to our civilization today, to our security and to our economy. just think of all the communications technology or the financial markets. without satellites, nothing works today. it is true that there is a strong security component here. we're not running away from that either. we have been able to establish a regular structured dialogue between the council and the commission, involving the european defence agency and the european satellite centre. this dialogue is intended to improve coordination between civil and security and defence related space activities. the gmes system, which is in the development phase, is the european response to the global ecological crisis. this system will provide us with the data and information we need to be able to act proactively and respond when disasters occur. overall, of course, our two flagship projects gmes and galileo are important contributions to the lisbon strategy, ensuring that europe's industrial and technological base for space-based applications remains strong. as regards gmes, i am very pleased to tell you that the commission has just adopted a communication on the organisation of funding and cooperation for gmes, following my proposal. the competitiveness council will be dealing with this in a few days. we can say that gmes is on the right track. the first demonstration projects have been launched. we'll be able to keep to the schedule, as far as i can see. we are in the best possible agreement with esa on the space-based infrastructure of gmes. the esa has already made great progress in developing the european satellites which we still need for this system. so it looks good. but one thing still needs to be regulated: we have only research funds available in the community budget for gmes as well. we don't have the operative equipment. we will need a small amount of operational funds for the first time next year, which has already been arranged with the budgetary authority. but we have to find a long-term solution here, because one thing is clear: gmes is not a system that will fund itself, there will be revenues, but they will never cover the costs. gmes is a european infrastructure project. it must be seen as such, and we must ensure long-term funding. we will be drawing up a detailed roadmap and action plan for the future implementation of the gmes initiative next year. in summary, the commission will present in 2009 a proposal for the financing of the first gmes missions in 2011 based on a detailed impact assessment and a cost-benefit analysis. galileo has already been mentioned. i would just like to say that thanks to the good cooperation between the institutions, the galileo and egnos programmes now have a solid legal basis and can become operational. the implementation of galileo and egnos is also planned, but it remains to be seen whether industry can meet the gnss regulation's requirement to complete the galileo system by 2013. this will be apparent during the bidding process. i would like to make a specific appeal to the european space industry to take advantage of the great opportunity that galileo offers and to work closely with us and to really mobilise all the forces and all the resources! galileo is one of our most important, if not the most important, industrial policy project, and we must ensure that it runs smoothly. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. it is true that different international regulations govern procurement practices in the space sector. these practices differ according to whether the goods are services or goods, but also and especially according to which countries have signed the relevant agreements. the commission has followed the principle of strict reciprocity in the promotion of the galileo r & d phase and we hope that this has given new impetus to the negotiations with third countries on mutual market opening. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am particularly concerned about this because we have very few european players in the field of space. the european union is not a mere institution, but a political one. but many others are contributing, and i am very pleased to see that in a number of member states, especially in new member states, there is a growing number of specialised space technology companies, small and mediumsized, which sometimes offer highly complex, very advanced services or products. it is therefore important to ensure that large projects take account of small and medium-sized enterprises in the award of contracts, with a corresponding share of 40% provided for, and the commission will do everything in its power to ensure that this share is respected. this is not just a purely economic issue, it is also a highly political one, because this is how we are going to ensure that european activities in space are not seen as a privilege of the few large european spacefaring countries, but that they can be understood as something that all 27 of us are doing and from which all 27 of us are also benefiting!

madam president, commissioner, the european union must be prepared to face the demographic challenge. social europe must be able to respond to the expectations of its citizens: quality education, an efficient and accessible health system, jobs that allow a decent life and the guarantee of a decent pension after a working life. the union's population is aging. at the same time, few member states have seen a rise in births, with ireland and france being the best performers, as a result of specific policies adopted. at the same time, although at community level the infant mortality rate has fallen to 4.7 per 1 000 inhabitants, there are still member states where it is 12 per 1 000 inhabitants. europe must invest in health, education and social protection. ensuring well-paid jobs means a decent life for workers, but also ensuring the resources needed to pay for pensions. the pension system is a system based on solidarity between generations.
inspections are an important element in ensuring the application and compliance with community environmental legislation. in this respect, the commission's recommendation to establish minimum criteria for environmental inspections in the member states was an important step forward when it was adopted in 2001. however, the evaluation of the application of this recommendation has raised several concerns. the commission's communication thus notes that there are still considerable differences in the way environmental inspections are carried out at local, regional and national level. in addition, it was found that the national measures adopted under that provision differed greatly in terms of both application and control. the shortcomings of this recommendation do not appear to be satisfactorily addressed in the commission communication. even if it aims to address the problems mentioned above, it avoids a key element that has caused the modest success of the recommendation, namely the very legal nature of this act. i therefore believe that a review of the recommendation alone will only maintain the current uncertainty. only a directive can bring about a substantial and effective improvement in environmental inspections.

in writing. − demographic projections that show the eu's working population to decline by 48 million by 2050 and that the dependency rate is set to double to 51% by 2050 indicate that in the future more immigrants with different skills and qualifications will be attracted to some member states to counterbalance these negative trends. the considerable differences in the criteria for defining and admitting highly qualified workers clearly limit their mobility across the european union, affecting the efficient redistribution of legally resident human resources and preventing the elimination of regional imbalances. as a representative of a member state which joined the european union in 2007, i voted in favour of this report, which will effectively address current and future demands for highly skilled labour, taking into account the principle of community preference applied to eu citizens.
in writing. − i voted for the amendment of the eu regulation establishing a medium-term financial assistance mechanism for member states' balance of payments; thus, the financial assistance ceiling was increased from eur 12 billion to eur 25 billion for eu member states not in the euro area experiencing balance of payments difficulties. the european parliament considers that non-euro area member states should be encouraged to seek possible medium-term financial support within the community to deal with their balance of payments deficit before seeking international support. the current situation is further evidence of the usefulness of the euro for the protection of the euro-area member states and invites the non-euro-area member states to join as soon as they meet the maastricht criteria.
in writing. − the dramatic decline in bee populations and, therefore, pollination is threatening fruit, vegetable and plant production in the european union. the decline in bee numbers is due both to various parasites and mites in the atmosphere and to pesticide spraying. the main problem is infection with the varroa parasite, which manifests itself in deformed wings and abdomen, underdeveloped bees, unable to fly and with a very short lifespan. left untreated, varroa can wipe out an entire bee colony in a matter of months. long-term use of pesticides has also contributed to the decline of bee populations, even when they were used to kill mycoses and parasites. some scientists believe that another cause is electromagnetic radiation from cell phones that infiltrates the bees' navigation system, rendering them unable to return to their hives. research in this area will need to be developed to find solutions to combat diseases affecting bees, and farmers' efforts to reduce the number of applications of plant protection products during flowering will also help to halt the decline of these insects.

on behalf of the alde group. – unless we achieve a truly common stance in the eu in favour of real reform, achieving adequate global rules for the financial markets becomes much harder. sensible people would say that a massive failure of both regulation and oversight, together with revealed flaws of an overly simplistic economic paradigm, provide an indubitable answer to what to do. but some still argue that soft regulations should be the norm of the new system. in my view, they are wrong, whether they honestly think so or are driven by parochial interests. one of keynes’ intellectual legacies – that highly volatile capital flows are inimical to trade and prosperity – has shown its relevance in the current huge mess and other crises, including in emerging markets. for decades now a mantra has been heard worldwide: that not much can be done in national policy-making because global markets would punish a government. but is the complexion of global financial markets god-given? are not global markets, aside from their technological drivers, also the product of human beings’ decisions to set rules for finance, trade and investment? the claim that nothing can be done about finance, when it brings about misery, is unconvincing. much can be done in regulating all financial entities (including hedge funds and private equity funds), constraining leverage, dealing with pro-cyclicality and accounting, coordinating policies better, dealing with the rating agencies. the decline of a paradigm which equates market economies with no regulations has to be seen in conjunction with a rising multi-polar economic world in the attempt to forge a new international financial system. on the latter hinges the fate of an open world economic system. unless we do the right things now, we run the risk of crippling our liberal democracies. i hope that the new american administration will be forthcoming in this respect. but we at home in europe have to rise to the momentousness of this period.

on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, this year we are celebrating the tenth anniversary of the eu code of conduct on arms exports. but even though this was a success at the time, we must now express our frustration and bitterness with the failure to make it a legally binding instrument. three years have passed since the council working group on arms reached a technical agreement on a common position. how many more years does the european council need to adopt it? how can we, as the european union, protect our own credibility when speaking against illegal arms trafficking, if we are not able to put our entire house in order? we need a code of conduct to be legally binding if we want to avoid any easy intra-community transfer of arms, which may tempt brokers to look for the weakest link in europe. when we speak of arms exports, we should think at the same time of human lives at stake in unstable countries. we can easily be accused, instead of peacemaking, of fuelling local conflicts in vulnerable parts of the world. i welcome the french defence minister’s declaration that france has withdrawn its reservation on the common position. will the french presidency be able to convince the other member states which are still opposing it? i can only hope so, and wish for the french presidency to make the adoption of the common position in the next two weeks another of the great achievements of its term of office.

in writing. the report in question is particularly important because it introduces mechanisms to eliminate or reduce the possibilities of budget fraud through fraudulent intra-community transactions involving vat. the annual damage caused by shell companies is currently estimated at €100 million (16% of the eu's own resources). the reduction of the time limits for both the collection of information and its transmission between the tax administrations of the member states is likely to contribute to a better monitoring of this type of transaction. the commission's proposal is to link the tax administrations of the member states to a common database to register the individuals behind the shell companies responsible for carrying out such fraudulent transactions. in this way, they will be prevented from setting up any other company in the whole of the european union and not just in one member state - as is happening now - by being identified in real time, by checking the database and, further, by the fact that the information reaches the trade register which has been asked to register a new company.

in writing. – social developments in the balkans in terms of gender equality have unfortunately been notorious for the lack of improvement in this field. even though some of the balkan countries have been given candidate status for eu membership, the situation of women is becoming increasingly worrisome and hardly improving. in order to sustain the relative position of women in the balkan societies, the eu must become more involved in the slow democratic process which characterises most countries in the region and encourage the fostering of legally binding instruments with regard to women’s rights and liberties. furthermore, positive discrimination should also be a concept employed by the governments in the region, in the same manner as in the eu member states that apply it. nevertheless, in order to recreate a stable post-conflict environment, it is imperative to promote the development of an equal society that protects the position of women while avoiding the re-establishment of the ‘patriarchal’ institutions that have characterised much of the past. the participation of women in the decision-making process is essential to achieving a substantial change in their status in society and will have concrete significance for future improvements.
in writing. the report on the situation of women in the balkans discusses one of the most topical issues: the place of women in contemporary society. the situation of women in the balkans is raising several alarming signs as the process of democratic stabilisation is under way. in addition to being exhaustive, the report covers essential and generally applicable chapters such as: women in the labour market, the fight against stereotypes, women's health, women in decision-making, violence against women and trafficking in human beings. these themes are all the more edifying in the context of countries that have undergone major changes in the last 20 years. the difficulty of assessing the situation in these countries is worrying. women are discriminated against, whether they want to or not. one example is the "unofficial" labour market for women, which is perceived as a state of normality in some countries. an even greater problem is found among women who are or are "oriented" toward activities beneath human dignity, such as prostitution, or fall prey to human trafficking. of concern is the fact that many women are also victims of domestic violence. in another line of thought, women need to be more involved in changing mindsets and taking their rightful place in society.

mr president, the eu has the potential to be a global leader in the fight against climate change and that is what our citizens are expecting from us. therefore it is crucial to reach a first-reading agreement on the climate change package, not only to meet those expectations but to go to copenhagen with a unified position. i would like to thank my colleagues who have been working long hours to try to achieve this. it is important to keep our ambitious targets, but at the same time we cannot ignore the dramatic impact of the financial crisis on the competitiveness of european industry, which has been greatly affected by it. given this new economic context, it is even more important to consider the wide variety of industrial infrastructures in member states and it should be recognised that some of them have achieved a rapid and large-scale reorganisation and modernisation. this is why we need to offer reasonable and appropriate flexibility to member states and industries to achieve their co2 emission reduction targets.
the european union has committed itself to finalising the 'climate change' dossier by january 2009. the outcome of the negotiations will be of particular importance at the united nations conference in poznań, where the union's commitment to reducing its carbon emissions and helping poorer nations will be assessed. we must ensure that the targets remain ambitious for the signing of an international agreement, so that developing countries are sufficiently motivated to follow our lead. increasing the target from 20% to 30% after 2020 should remain a priority in the event of an international agreement, even if this transition is made through renegotiation. a more ambitious long-term objective will ensure the credibility of the european union as the main actor in the fight against global warming and lead to favourable outcomes in the forthcoming copenhagen negotiations.
in writing. the european commission adopted the package of legislative proposals on climate change and renewable energy on 23 january 2008. the package allocates to member states, by criteria and targets, the eu's targets agreed at the 2007 spring european council, namely to reduce greenhouse gas (ghg) emissions by at least 20% by 2020 at eu level and to increase the share of renewable energy in total energy consumption by 20% and to increase energy efficiency by 20% by the same time. you can negotiate on all planes, but you can't negotiate with nature. meeting these commitments - to reduce ghg emissions and increase the share of renewable resources - therefore involves major structural reforms in all economic sectors. the assumption by romania of the national obligations arising from the legislative package will generate important economic and social effects. the completion of the negotiations on the 'climate change' package represents an opportunity to balance tackling climate change, strengthening supplier security and promoting competitiveness, growth and job creation.
in writing. we are pleased that the negotiations between the european parliament and the council on the 'climate change - renewable energy' package are now moving towards consensus. the european council of 11-12 december 2008 will decide on all elements related to this package. in preparation for the 11-12 december talks, romania together with slovakia, hungary, bulgaria, lithuania and latvia submitted on 28 november a proposal to redistribute the revenues from co2 auctions according to the following formula: (90 x) % + 10 % + x %, where x is distributed to those ms that in 2005 had more than 20% reductions in the kyoto emission ceiling. romania also considers that the review clause in 2014 is absolutely necessary, without however calling into question the 20% reduction targets (or the 10% target), precisely to allow for possible adjustments of the mechanisms, depending on the concrete conditions of the period in question (which cannot be foreseen now).
in writing. − i voted for this report because the agreement aims to contribute to the effective enforcement of competition law by promoting cooperation between competition authorities and reducing the likelihood of conflicts. korea is the eu's fourth largest non-european trading partner and the eu is the largest foreign investor in korea. given the growing importance of this partnership, it seems appropriate to include korea alongside the other three partners with whom the ec has signed agreements on cooperation on anti-competitive practices. the agreement provides for notification of enforcement activities by one of the competition authorities that could affect the important interests of the other party, mutual assistance, including the possibility for one party to request the other party to take enforcement action, coordination of enforcement activities, and the exchange of information. confidentiality measures are also provided for. in a broader perspective, the importance of multilateral trade and multilateral competition rules for the achievement of free and open cross-border markets should be emphasised.

in writing. - the report seems to me extremely important, given the need for harmonisation of legislation in the eu member states in many areas, including maintenance obligations. the revised version of the regulation on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments and cooperation in matters of maintenance obligations clearly states the criteria and situations when such an obligation is imposed by law. the maintenance obligation is personal and successive, personal and unilateral. the regulation simplifies the life of citizens of the european union states on the procedure for establishing maintenance obligations. more specifically, once the judgment is given in one member state, it will produce equal and binding effects in all member states, which is essential if we consider that many citizens are domiciled in a member state other than the one in which they were born or in which the maintenance decision was given.
in writing. − this regulation will simplify citizens' lives. simplification was desirable, first of all, as regards the procedure for establishing maintenance obligations. thus, the regulation provides that, once a maintenance judgment has been given in the member states, it produces binding effects in all member states. it also provides for the organisation of an operational system of cooperation between the central authorities of the member states to help creditors recover amounts owed to them. the final result, which we are facing, is a compromise that enjoys our support. this would allow eu citizens to benefit from it as soon as possible. as regards the implementation procedures, the european commission must continue its work. we can only rejoice to hear that there is such an intention and hope that in this way citizens will be able to reap the benefits as soon as possible. however, effective implementation is the cornerstone that would ensure the existence of a common, harmonised system for the recognition and enforcement of maintenance decisions in the european union.

social europe must guarantee every european citizen a decent living on his or her salary. decent work must ensure a decent living. respect for an employee involves setting a work schedule and a rest period that allow the employee to rest and spend sufficient time with his family. children need parental guidance and supervision, and the lack or diminishment of time spent with the family can have negative consequences on the children's education. no employer should be able to require an employee to work more than 48 hours a week. i think that the working time directive should deal more closely with the specific situation of medical staff on duty. i support the report by mr cercas, which protects the interests of employees without ignoring the legitimate interests of employers, by giving them the possibility of adapting their working time to their needs. i also welcome the amendments which stress the importance of collective agreements.
in the current context of the financial crisis, which has direct effects on the economic and social lives of european citizens, the working time directive is a key element of european social policies. mr cercas' report is a rational and consistent approach to the process of evaluating the conclusions on the application of the directive at member state level. the directive is now a flexible instrument, setting a level of protection below which action cannot be authorised to the detriment of the health and safety of workers.
during the long debate on this report, a concern was expressed - that the majority obtained at the first reading could not be achieved at the vote tomorrow, because those who have joined in the meantime would have changed the balance of power in this chamber. it is very true that in the council the right-wing governments have the same position regardless of geographical position, east or west. but something else needs to be clarified. eastern workers are equally firm in supporting all the amendments proposed by the european parliament and rejected by the council. the trade unions in romania, for example, will also be represented here tomorrow in strasbourg, aware that the rights won are not won once and for all and must always be defended. their message is simple: to the existing problems, a much more effective solution than no-limit work is to stop the unlimited enrichment of low-paid labor, including that of eastern workers.
in writing. i welcome the affirmation in this report of the social vision of the european left, with the representatives of the socialists rightly criticising the violation, by allowing voluntary exclusion clauses from working time, of the principle of no derogation from legislation on the health and safety of employees at work. while flexible working hours, based on the nature of the work and the abilities of each person, might be beneficial, i cannot help but think of the many abuses suffered by employees. i am referring to the case of romania, where overtime is neither calculated nor legally paid in many cases, where overtime is not the result of an employee-employer agreement but of the employer's discretionary will, not to mention the endangerment of the health and even the lives of those who have entered a maze from which they can only emerge at the risk of losing their jobs. the pretext of stimulating labour competitiveness often hides exploitation. i think it's preferable to limit this to 48 hours. as regards duty time, i consider it unfair that 'the idle period of duty time' should not be considered as working time and, therefore, paid.
the european works council and the procedure for informing and consulting workers in undertakings or groups of undertakings are indispensable instruments for the protection of employees. the works councils must be very active, especially in situations of company restructuring. in the case of multinational companies or groups of companies, it is essential that the employees of the company in the member state where the redundancies occur are consulted and sit at the negotiating table. where a group of undertakings takes important decisions concerning the future of the undertaking and its employees, the employees of the undertaking in the member state where the restructuring takes place must be informed and be able to participate and influence the decision taken. until now, the european community has only provided financial assistance to firms in restructuring situations. i think that this assistance should also be given to dismissed employees.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, what are the lessons of the french presidency? there's three of them. lesson one. the european union needs a strong presidency, exercised for a longer period of time in relation to the processes it has to manage, and by a dynamic and competent personality who can devote himself entirely to european interests and affairs. so we need at least the lisbon treaty. europe must not be personalized, it is true, but it must be personalized. lesson two. the european union needs a presidency which is able to forge compromises between the representatives of the nations, relying on the representatives of the european citizens. so we need a stronger parliament because a united europe does not threaten the nation states. it is anarchy and neo-feudal fragmentation which constitute the inevitable alternative to european integration and which threaten the integrity of nations. lesson three. the european union needs economic governance that balances sustainable growth with social solidarity and cohesion, and if a multi-speed europe, even if undesirable, proves inevitable, this europe must be structured according to the difference in political will and not according to the level of economic development. for the rest, congratulations and thanks. to every lord, all honor.

in writing. the european council recently discussed the energy-climate change legislative package. the main concern was the financial and economic crisis. we cannot ignore the food crisis that is involved. in europe today, economically viable agriculture is a necessary condition for ensuring food security for its population. i understand the concerns of my colleague, mr turmes, about biofuels and the opposition to the 10% target for biofuels, supported by the commission. there are voices that blame energy crops for the food crisis and the rising food prices. however, these crops account for only 2% of current agricultural production in europe. there is a risk that an unjustified increase in biofuel production will compete with food production. this risk can be countered by well-defined legislation and by setting precise targets in national action plans. we can't ignore the benefits of using biofuels, like reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, reducing greenhouse gas emissions. in countries with high agricultural potential, such as romania, bulgaria or poland, the use of biofuels is a viable socioeconomic alternative for rural development and environmental protection by exploiting the potential of energy efficiency and renewable energies.

in writing. the outcome of the climate package negotiations between the three institutions represents a balanced compromise that will help the european union make a significant contribution to measures to combat global warming, the first bloc of states to make this commitment through legally binding commitments. we are now in a global financial crisis which has caused concern in most member states about the target of reducing carbon emissions, but the outcome of the summit is a balanced agreement between the need to protect the climate and the need to overcome this economic impasse. in my view, the use of arguments relating to this crisis should not prevent the adoption of the package and i hope that all the political groups in parliament will give it a positive vote. i am pleased that countries that reduced their emissions between 1990 and 2005, including romania, have been recognised for their efforts by changing the distribution grid for auction revenues without changing the overall structure of the package. i also believe that most of the elements of the ets directive that have created significant problems for member states have been addressed correctly and that the end result has been a fair one that will launch the european union into a real mission to combat climate change.
